# 0•4 Advanced driving

![](images/b0801bcaef846b9d8af09fcf5be113d278593fbf057b33e0c5407d527e1735e2.webp)

Many people sae the words "advanced driving' and believe that it won't interest them or that it is a style of driving beyond their own abiities. Nothing could be further from the truth.Advanced -driving is straightforward safe, sensible driving - the sort of driving we should all do every time we get bebind the wheel.

An average of 10 people are klied every day on UK roads and 870 more ane injured, some seriously, Lives are ruined daily, usually because somebody did something stupid. Something like 95% of all accidents are due to human error, mostly driver tailure. Sometimes we make genuine mistakes - everyone does. Sometimes we have lapses of concentration,  Sometimes we deliberately take risks.

For many people, the process of leaming to drive' doesn't go much furher than leaming how to pass the driving test because of a common belief that good drivers are made by 'experience“.

Leaming to drive by 'experience' teaches three driving skills:

Quick reections,  (Whoops, that wes closel   
Good handling skils, (Horn, swerve, brake, horn).   
Reliance on vehicle technology-(Great stulf this ABS, stop in no distance even in the wet...)

Drivers whose skills are 'experience based" generally have a lot of near misses and the odd aocident,  The results can be seen every day in our courts and our hospital casualty departments.

Advanced drivers have leamt to control the risks by controling the position and speed of their vehicke. They avoid accidents and near misses, even i the drivers around them make mistakes.

The key skilis of advanced driving are concentration, effective all-round observation, anticipation and planning. When good vehicle handling is added to these skills, all driving situations can be approached and negotiated in a safe. methodical way, leaving nothing to chance:

Concentration means applying your mind to safe driving, completely excluding anything that's not relevant. Driving is usually the most dangercus activity that most of us undertake in our dally routines. I1 deserves our full attention.

Observation means not just looking, but seeing and seeking cut the infommation found in the driving environment,

Anticipation means asking yoursell what is happening, what you can reasonably expect to happen and what could happen unexpectedly,  (One of the commonest words used in compiling accident reports is suddenly'.)

Planning is the link between seeing something and taking the appropriata actian. For many drivers, planning is the missing link.

If you want to become a sater and more skatul driver and you want ta enjoy your driving more, contact the institute of Advanced Motorists on 0208 994 4403 or write to IAM House, Chiswick High Roed, London We <hs for an information pack:

The Citroen Xsara range was launched in five-door Hatchback form in the Autumn of 1997 as a replacement for the Citroen ZX, Originaly, the Xsara was avalabie with various engine options, depending on model and country of export. The initial engine ineup included 1.4 itre (1360cc), 1.6 litre (1587cc) and 1.8 litre (1 761cc) petrol engines. and 1.9 litre (1905cc) diesel and turbo diesel engines.

in early 1998 the Xsara range was further enhanced by the addition of a three-door Coupe model, followed soon after by an Estate model. Further developments -and improvements to the existing engines continued, mainly in the area of emission controi to meet increasingly stringent European legislation.

in 1999 a new 1,9 litre (1868cc) diesel engine was introduced to replace the existing 1.9 litre non-turbo unit, and a 2.0 litre (1998cc) 16-valve petrol engine also became available for certain export countries.

For the 2000 model year another ail new turbocharged diesel engine was introduced, this being the 2.0 litre (1997cc) Nigh pressure dieselinjection (HDi unit,

All engines are derived from the well-proven TU and XU series petrol engines, and XUD series diesel engines, which have appeared in many Citroen and Peugeot vehicles (the DW series diesel enaine is essentially an XUD unit with revised cylinder head),. The engines are all of four-cylinder singleor double-overhead camshatt design, mounted transversely at the front of the car, with the transmission mounted on the left-hand side. All models have a five-speed manual transmission with the option of  a four-speed  automatic transmission on certain petrol engines.

All models have fully-independent front suspension, The rear suspension is semiindependent, with torsion bars and traiting aтms.

A wide range of standard and optional equipment is availble within the Xsara range to suit most tastes, including power steering. central locking, engine immobiliser, eectric windows, electric sunnoof, and air bags. An anti-lock braking system and ar conditioning system are available as options, or standard equipment on certain models,

Provided that regular servicing is caried out in accordance with the manufacturer's recommendations, the Citroen Xsara should prove rellable and very economical, The engine compartment is well-designed, and most of the items requiring frequent attention are easily accessible.

# Your Citron Xsara Manual

The aim o this manual is to help you get the best value fron your vehicle, It can do so in several ways. It can heip you decide what work must be done (even should you choose to get it done by a garage), provide information on routine maintenance and servicing, and give a logical caurse of action and diagnosis when random faults occur. However, it is hoped that you will use the manual by tacking the work yourselt. On simpler jobs it may even be quicker than booking the car into a garage and going there twice, to leave end colliect it. Perhaps most important, a lot of money can be saved by avoiding the costs a garage must charge to cover its labour and overheads,

The manual has drawings and descriptions to show the function of the various components so that their layaut can be understood. Tasks are descnbed and photographed in a clear step-by-step sequence.

References to the "left-hand' and 'righthand' sides of the vehicle are always in the sense of when viewed by a person sat in the driver's seat, facing fonwards.

Puddles on the garage floor or drive, or obvious wetness under the bonnet or underneath the car, suggest a leak that needs investigating, It can sometimes be difficult to decide where the leak is coming from, especially if the engine bay is very dirty aiready. Leaking oll or fuld can also be blown rearwaras by the passage of air under the car, giving a false impression of where the problem lies.

A

Waming: Most automotive olls and fuids are poisonous. Wash them off skin, and change out of contaminated clothing. without delay.

# Towing

When al eise fals, you may find yoursell having to get a tow home - or of course you may be helping somebody else. Longdistance recovery should only be done by a garage or breakdown service, For shorter distances, DIY towing using another car is easy enaugh. but observe the following points:

Use a proper tow-rope — they are not expensive. The vehicle being towed must display an ON TOW sign in Its rear window. Always turn the ignition key to the "on' position when the vehicle is being towed, so that the steering lock is released, and that the direction indicator and brake lights will work.

Only attach the tow-rope to the towing eye provided. This can be found in the luggage compartment next to the wheelbrace, and is screwed into the front or rear towing locations on the body, as required. Use the wheelbrace to screw the towing eye firmly into place.

Before being towed, release the handbrake and select neutral on the transmission.

On models with automatic transmission, If towing with the whaels on the ground, special precautions apply, An acditional 1.0 litre of the specified automatic transmission fluid must be added to the transmission before towing. The towing speed must be limited to 30 mph (48 kph) and the distance must not exceed 30 miles (48 km). On completion, the transmission fluid level must be returnad to the nomal amount, I in doubi, do not tow, or transmission damage may result.

Note that greater-than-ususl pedal pressure will be required to operate the brakes, since the vacuum servo unit is only operational with the engine running.   
Greater-than-usual steering effort will also be required.   
The driver of the car being towed must keep the tow-rope taut at all times to avoid snatching.   
Make sure that both drvers know the route before setting off.   
Oniy drive at moderate speeds and keep the distance towed to a minimum. Orive smoothly and allw plenty of time for slowing down at junctions.

# Tyre condition and pressure

it is very important that tyres are in good condition, and at the corect pressure - having a tyre falure at any speed is highly dangeraus. Tyre wear is influenced by driving style - hansh braking and acceleration, or tast corering. will all produce more rapid tyre wear. As a general rule, the front tyres wear out faster than the rears, Interchanging the tyres from tront to rear ("rotating" the tyres) may result in more even wear." However. I' this is completely etfective, you may have the expense of replacing al four tyres at once!

Remove any nails or stones embedded in the tread before they penetrate the tyre to cause deflation. If removal of a nal does reveal that the tyre has been punctured, refit the nail so that its point of penetration is marked. Then immediately change the wheel, and have the tyre repaired by a tyre dealer.

Regularly check the tyres for damage in the form of cuts or bulges, especially in the sidewalls. Periodically remove the wheels. and clean any dirt or mud from the inside and outside surfaces: Examine the wheel rims for signs of rusting, corrosion ar other damage. Light alloy wheeis are easily damaged by "kerbing" whilst parking; steel wheels may aiso become dented or buckled, A new wheel is very ohten the only way to avercome severe damage.

New tyres should be balanced when they are fitted, but it may become necessary to rebalance them as they wear, or if the balance weights fitted to the wheel rim should tal oft. Unbalanced tyres will wear more quickly, as wil the steering and suspension components. Wheel imbalance is normally signiflied by vibration, particularly at a certain speed (typicaly around 50 mph), i this vibration is felt anly through the steering, then it is sikely that just the front wheelis need balancing. If. hawever, the vibration is felt through the whole car, the rear wheels could be out of balance. Wheel balancing should be camied out by a tyre dealer or garage.

# Choosing your engine oil

Engines need of, not only to lubricate moving parts and minimise wear, but also to maximise power output and to improve fuel economy. By introducing a simplitied and improved range of engine oils, Duckhams has taken away the confusion and made it easier for you to choose the night ol for your engine.

# HOW ENGINE OIL WORKS

# • Beating friction

Without oll the moving surtaces inside your engine will rub together, heat up and melt, quickly causing the engine to seize. Engine oil creates a fim which separates these moving parts, preventing wear and heat buld-up.

# • Cooling hot-spots

Temperatures inside the engine can exceed 1000° C. The engine ol circulates and acts as a coolant, transfering heat from the hot-spots to the sump.

# • Cleaning the engine internally

Good qualty engine oils clean the inside of your engine, collecting and dispersing combustion deposits and cantroling them unti they are trapped by the oif fiter or flushed out at oi change.

# OIL CARE - FOLLOW THE CODE

To handle and dispose of used engine ol safely, always:

. Avoid skin contact with used engine oil. Repeated or prolonged contact can be harmful.

OILCARE . 080066 33 66

Dispose of used oll and empty packs in a responsible manner in an authorised disposal site. Call 0800 663366 to find the one nearest to you. Never tip oi down drains or onto the ground.

# DUCKHAMS ENGINE OILS

For the driver who demands a premlum quality oil for complete reassurance, we recommend synthetic formula Duckhams QXR Premium Engine Oils.

For the driver who requires a straightforward quality engine oil, we recammend Duckhams Hypergrade Engine Oiis.

The maintenance intervals in this manual are provided with the assumption that you, not the dealer, will be carrying out the work. These are the minimum maintenance intervals recommended for vehicles driven daily, If you wish to keep your vehicle in peak condition at al times, you may wish to perform some of these procedures more often, We encourage frequent maintenance, because i enhances the efficiency, performance and resale value of your vehicle.

If the vehicle is driven in dusty areas, used to tow a traller, or driven frequenty at slow speeds (dling in traftic) or on short joumeys, more Irequent maintenance intervals ane necommended.

When the vehicle is new, It should be serviced by a lactorysuthorised dealer service department, in order to preserve the tactory warranty,

Vaive clearance checking is no longer specified as par of the routine maintenance schedule. Check the valve clearances if there is any tapping or rattling from the top of the engine, or in the event of an unexplained lack of performance. The prudent owner may wish to. check the clearances more often, pemaps at 25 000 mile (4ó 000 km) or two-yearly intervals.

# Every 25 000 miles (40 000 km) or 2 years – whichever comes first

In adobion to al ine items listed above, carry out the following:

Operate and lubricate all hinges and locks   
(Section 16).   
Renew the automatic transmission fluid – 4 HP 14 transmission only (Section 17).   
Renew the air filter (Section 18).   
Check the condition of the rear brake shoes   
models with rear drum brakes (Section 19).   
Check the operation of the handbrake (Section 20). Renew the brake fluid (Section 21).

# Every 250 miles (400 km) or weekly

Refer to Weekly checks

# Every 12 500 miles (20 000 km) or 12 months – whichever comes first

Renew the engine oil and fiter (Section 3).   
Check all underbonnet/underbody components for fluid leaks (Section 4).   
Check the condition of the auxiliary drivebelt   
(Section 5).   
Check the clutch control mechanism (Section 6). Renew the pollen fiter (Section 7).   
Check the condition of the driveshaft rubber   
gaiters (Section 8).   
Check the steering and suspension components (Section 9).

# Routine maintenance – petrol engine models1•

# 1General information

This Chapter is designed to help the home mechanic maintain his/her vehicle for safety, economy, long Ie and peak performance.

The Chapter contains a master maintenance schedule, followed by Sections dealing specifically with, each task in the schedule. Visual checks, adjustmerits, component renewal and other heilpful items ars included. Reter to the accompanying illustrations of the engine compartment and the underside of the vehicle for the locations of the various companents.

Servicing your vehicle in accordance with the mileage/time maintenance schedule and the following Sections will pravide a planned maintenance programme, which should result in a long and reliable service life. This is a comprehensive plan, so maintaining some items but not others at the specified service intervals wil not produce the same results.

As you service your vehicle, you will discover that many of the procedures can - and should - be grouped together, because of the particular procedune being pertormed, or because of the proximity of iwo otherwiseunrelated companents to one another, For example, if the vehicle is raised for any reason, the exhaust can be inspected at the same time as the suspension and steering components,

The first step in this maintenance programme is to prepare yourselt before the actual work begins. Read through all the Sections relevant to the work to be camied out, then make a list and gather allthe parts and tools required. if a problem is encountered, seek advice from a parts specialist, or a dealer service department

# Service interval display

Certain Xsara models are equipped with a service interval display indicator in the instrument panel When the ignition is initially switched on, a spanner appears in the display window and the total number of miles remaining until the next service is due is also shown.

The display should not necessarly be used as a definitive guide to the senvicing needs of your Xsara, but it is useful as a reminder, to ensure that servicing is not accidentally overooked, Owners of older cars, or those covering a small annual mileage, may feel inclined to service their car mone often, in which case the service interval display is perhaps less relevant.

The display should be reset whenever a service is caried out, and this is achieved using the trip meter reset button on the instrument panel as follows.

With the ignition switched off, press and hold down the trip meter reset button. Switch the ignition on and the mileage remaining untl the next service will flash, Continue to hold the button down for a turther ten seconds. The spanner symbol will disappear and the mileage will retumn to zero.

# Regular maintenance

1 H, from the time the vehicle is new, the routine maintenance schedule is followed closely, and frequent checks are made of fluid levels and high-wear tems, as suggested throughout this manual, the engine will be kept in reatively good running condition, and the need for additional work will be minimised. 2 It is possible that there will be times when the engine is running poorly due to the lack of regular maintenance. This is even more likaly if a used vehicle, which has not received regular and frequent maintenance checks, is purchased. In such cases, additional work may need to be caried out, outsice of the regular maintenance intervais,

3 Petrol eaks are diflicult to pinpoint, unless the leakage is significant and nence easily visible. If you suspect that there is a fuel leak from the area of the engine bay, leave the vehicle ovemight then start the engine from cold,  with the bonnet open,  Metal components tend to shrink when they are cold, and rubber seals and hoses tend to harden, so any leaks will be more apparent whilst the engine is warming up from a cold start.

Also check the area araund the fuel injectors for signs of O-ring leakage.

by making use of the vacuum is the inlet manifold, generated by the engine. Vacuum is ported to the servo by means of a large-bore hose, Any leaks that develop in this hose wil reduce the effectiveness of the braking system, and may affect the running of the engine.

Care must be taken to avoid contacting hot or moving components, as the engine must be running when testing in this manner. Renew any vacuum hoses that ace found to be defective.

# Radiator flushing

11 To fush the radiator, disconnect the top and bottom hoses and any other relevant hoses from the radiator, with reterence to Chapter 3.

12Insert a garden hose into the radiator top inlet. Direct a flow of clean water through the radiator, and continue flushing until clean water emerges from the nediator bottom outlet.

# Engine flushing

Temporarily refit the thermostat cover, without the thermostat. 15 with the top and bottom hoses disconnected from the radiator, insert a garden hose into the radiator top hose. Direct a clean flow of water through the engine, and continue flushing until clean water emerges from the nadator bottom hose.

16 When fushing is complete,  refit the thermostat and reconnect the hoses with relerence to Chapter 3.

These are the minimum maintenance intervals recommended for vehicles driven deily. If you wish to keep your vehicle in peak condition at all times, yau may wish to perform same of these procedures more often. We encourage frequent maintenance, because it enhances the efficiency, perfornance and resale value of your vehicle.

I the vehicle is diven in dusty areas, used to tow e trailer, or driven frequently at slow speeds idling in traffic or on short joureys, more frequent maintenance intervals are recommended.

When the vehicle is new, it should be senviced by a factory-authorised dealer service department, in order to preserve the factory wamanty.

Vame clearance checking is no longer specifed as part of the routine maintenance schedule, Check the valve clearances If there is any tapping or ratting from the top of the engine, or in the event of an unexplained leck of performance. The prudent owner may wish to check the clearances more often, peraps at 20 000 mile (30 000 km) or two-yeary intervals.

# 1 General information

This Chapter is designed to help the home mechanic maintain his/her vehicle for safety, ecanomy, long life and peak performance.

The Chapter contains a master maintenance schedule, followed by Sections dealing specifically with each task in the schedule. Visual  checks,  edjustments, component renewal and other helptul items are included. Refer to the accompanying llustrations of the engine compartment and the underside of the vehicle for the locations of the various components.

Servicing your vehicle in accordance with the mileage/time maintenance schedule and the following Sections will provide a planned maintenance programne, which should nesult in a long and reliable service life. This is a comprehensive plan, so maintaining some items but not others at the specifiad service intenvals wil not produce the same results.

As you service your vehicle, you will discover that many of the procedures can — and should — be grouped together, because of the particular procedure being performed, or because of the proximity of two otherwiseunrelated components to one another, For example, if the vehicle is raised for any reason, the exhaust can be inspected at the same time as the suspension and steering components.

The first step in this maintenance programme is to prepare yourself before the actual work begins. Read through all the Sections relevant to the work to be caried out, then make a list and gather all the parts and tools required. If a problem is encountered, seak advice from a parts specialist,  or a dealer service department.

# Service interval display

Certain Xsara models are equipped with a service interval display indicator in the instrument panel, When the ignition is initially switched on, a spanner appears in the display window and the total number of miiee remaining untl che next senice is due, is also shown.

The display should not necessarly be used as a definitive guide to the servicing needs of your Xsara, but it is useful as a reminder, to ensure that servicing is  not accidentally avericoked, Owners of alder cars, or those covering a small annual mileage, may feel inclined to service their car more often, in which case the service interval display is pemaps less relevant.

The display should be reset whenever a service is camied out, and this is achieved using the trip meter reset button on the instrument panel as follows.

With the ignition switched off, press and hold down the tip meter reset button. Switch the ignition on and the mileage remaining untll the next service will flash. Continue to hold the button down for a further ten seconds. The spanner symbol will disappear and the mlleage wil retum to zero.

# Regular maintenance

1 I, from the time the vehicle is new, the routine maintenance schedule is followed closely, and frequent checks are made of fuid levels and nigh-wear items, as suggested throughout this manual, the engine willi be kept in relatively good running condition, and the need for additional work will be minimised. 2 It is possibie that there will be times when the engine is running poory due to the lack o! regular maintenance. This is even more likely if a used vehicle, which has not received regular and frequent maintenance checks, is purchased, in such cases, additional work imay need to be carried out, outside of the regular maintenance intervals.

3 If engine wear is suspected, a compression test or leakdown test (refer to the relevant Part of Chapter 2) will provide valuable information regarding the overall perfornance of the main intemal components. Such a test can be used as a basis to decide on the extent af the work to be caried out. Iif, for exampla, a compression or leakdown test  indicates serious internal engine wear, conventional maintenance as described in this Chapter will not greatly improve the pertormance of the engine, and may prove a waste of time and money, unless extensive overhaul work is caried out finst.

# Vacuum hoses

18 Although the braking system Is hydraulically-operated, the brake servo unit amplifies the effort applied at the brake pedal, by making uae of the vacuum generated by the engine-driven vacuum pump. Vacuum is ported to the serva by means of a large-bore hose. Any leaks that develop in this hose will seriously reduce the effectiveness of the braking system.

1  In addiion, a number of the underbonnet components,  particularly the emission control components, are driven by vacuum supplied trom the vacuum pump via narowbore hoses, A leak in a vacuum hose means that air is being drawn into the hose (rather than escaping from If) and this makes leakage very difficult to detect. One method is to use an old length of vacuum hose as a kind of stethoscope – nold one end close to (but not in) your ear and use the other end to probe the area around the suspected leak, When the end of the hose is directly over a vacuum leak, a hissing sound will be heard cleanly through the hose. Care must be taken to avoid contacting hot or moving components, as the engine must be running, when testing in this manner, Renew any vacuum hoses that are tound to be defective.

# 10 Steering and suspension check

# Front suspension and steering check

1 Firmly apply the handbrake, then jack up the front of the car and support it securely on axle stands (see Jecking end vehicle support]. 2 Visually inspect the balljoint dust covers and the steering rack-and-pinion gaiters for splits, chafing or deterioration, Any wear of these componerts will cause loss of lubricarnt, together with dint and water entry, nesulting in rapid deterioraton of the baljoints or steering gaar.

3 On vehicles with power steering, check the fluid hoses for chafing or deterioration, and the pipe and hose unions for fuid leaks. Aiso check for sigas of fluid leakage under pressure: from the steering gear rubber gaiters, which would indicate faled fluld seals within the steering gear.

4 Grasp the roadwheel at the 12 o'dock and 6 o'clock positions, and try to rock it (see Illustration). Very slight free play may be fet, but if the movement is appreciable, further investigation is necessery to determine the source. Continue rocking the wheel while an assistant depresses the footbrake, If the movement is now aliminated or signiticantly reduced, it is likely that the hub bearings are at fault if the free play is stil evident with the footbrake depressed, then there is wear in the suspension joints or mountings.

5 Now grasp the wheel at the 9 o'clock and 3 o'clock positions, and try to nock it as before. Any movement felt now may again be caused by wear in the hub bearings or the steering track-rod baljoints. If the inner or outer baljaint is wom, the visuel movement will be obvious.

6 Usina a large sorewdrver or fat bar, check tor wear in the suspension mounting bushes by levering between the neievant suspension component and its attachment point, Some movement is to be expected as the mountings are made of rubber,  but  excessive wear should be abviaus, Also check the condition of any visible rubber bushes, looking for splits, cracks or contamination of the rubber.

7 With the car standing on its wheels, have an assistant tum the steering wheel back and forth about an eighth of a tum each way. There should be very little, if any, lost movement between the steering wheel! and roadwheels. I this is not the case, closely obsenve the joints and mountings previously desonbed, but in addition, check the steering column universal joints for wear, and the rackand-pinion steenng gear itself.

# Suspension strut/shock absorber check

8 Check for any signs of fuid leakage around the suspension strut/shock absorber body, or from the rubber galtr around the piston rod. Should any fluid be noticed, the suspenslon strut/shock absorber is defective intemally. and should be renewed. Note: Suspenslon struts/shock absorbers should always be renewed in pairs on the same axle.

9 The efficiency  of  the  suspension strut/shock absorber may be checked by bouncing the vehicle at each comer. Generally speaking, the body will return to its normal position and stop atter being depressed. If it rises and returns on a rebound, the suspension strut/shock absorber is probably suspect, Examine also the suspension strut/shock absorber upper and lower mountings for any signs of wear,

# 11 Front brake pad condition check

1 Firmly apply the handbrake, then jack up the front of the car and support it securely on axle stands (see Jacking and vehicle support). Remove the front roadwheels.

2 It is now posslble to check the thickness of the pad friction material (see Haynes Hint). If any pad's friction material is worn to the specified thickness or less, al four peds muat be ronewed as a set.

3 For a compreheneive check, the brake pads should be removed and cleaned. The operation of the caliper can then be checked, and the brake disc itself can be fully examined on bath sides. Refer to Chapter 9 for details.

# Instruments and electrical equipment

1 Check the operation of all instruments and electrical equipment,

# Steering and suspension

3 Check for any abnormaltes In the steering. suspension, handing or road "feel', 4 Drive the vehicle, and check that there are no unusual vibrations or noises. s Check that the steering feeis positive, with no excessive 'sloppiness', or roughness, and check for any suspension noises when comering, or when driving over bumps.

# Drivetrain

6 Check the performance of the engine, clutch, transmission and driveshafts.

7 Listen for any unusual noises from the engine, clutch and transmission,

8 Make sure that the engine runs smoothly when idling, and that there is no hesitation when acoelerating.

9 Check that the clutch action is smooth and progressive, that the drive is taken up smoothly, and that the pedal travel is not excessive. Also listen for any noises when the clutch pedal is depressed,

10 Check that afl gears can be engaged smoothly, without noise, and that the gear lever action is smooth and not abnormally vague or 'notchy'.

11 Listen for a metalic clicking sound from the front of the vehicle, as the vehicle is civen siowly in a circle with the steering on ful lock. Cary out this check in both directions. If a clicking noise is heard, this indicates lack of lubrication or wear in a driveshaft constant velocity joint (see Chapter 8).

# Check the operation and performance of the braking system

12 Make sure that the vehicle does not pul to one side when braking, and that the wheels do not lock prematurely when braking hard.

13 Check that there is no vibration through the steering when braking.

14 Check  that  the handbrake operates corectly, without excessive movement of the lever, and that it holds the vehicle stationary on a slope.

15 Test the operation of the brake servo unit as folows. With the engine off, depress the footbrake four or five times to exhaust the vacuum. Star the engine, holding the braka pedal depressed. As the engine starts, there should be a noticeable 'give' in the brake pedal as vacuum bulds up. Allow the engine to run for at least two minutes, and then switch it of If the brake pedal is depressed now, it should be possible to detect a hiss from the servo as the pedal is depressed. After about four or five applications, no further hissing should be heard, and the pedal should teel considerably finmer.

# 1 General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the TU series petrai engines. Simllar information covering the XU series petrol engines, and  the  diesel engines will be found in Chapters 28 to 2D. All procedures concerning engine removal and refiting. and engine biock/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chaoters 2E and 2F as applicable,

Aefer to Vehicle ldertfication in the Raferance Section of this manual for details of engine code locations.

Most of the operations included in Chapter 2A are based on the assumption that the engine is sti instalied in the car, Therefore, # this information is being used during a complete engine overhaul, with the engine already removed, many of the steps included here will nat apply.

# TU series engine description

The TU series engine is a well-proven engine wtich has been fitted to many previous Citroën and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of the in-line four-cylinder, ovemead cershaf (OHC) type, mounted Iransversely at the front of the car,  with the transmission attached to its left-hand end. The Xsara range is, fited with both 1.4 Iire (13eacc) and 1.6 itre (1587cc) versions of the engine.

The crankshaft nuns in tive main bearings. Thrustwashers are fitted to No 2 main bearing (upper half) to control crankshaft endfioat.

The connecting rods rotate on horizontallysplit bearing shelis at their big-ends. The pistons are attached to the connecting rods by gudgeon pins, which are an interference fit in the connecting rod small-end eyes. The aluminium-alloy pistons are itted with three piston rings — two compression ings and an oll controi nng.

On 1.4 litre engines, the cylinder block is made of aluminium,  and replaceable wet iners are fited to the cylinder bores, Sealing

![](images/eac11911d37bb3d191c5d01c7b35e65016d0a05d62e37b7a8b841846aa4fbfc5.webp)  
1.12 Engine code is stamped on a plate (arrowed) attached to the front of the cylinder block — viewed from above

O-rings are tited at the base of each liner, to prevent the escape of coolant into the sump.

On 1.6 litre engines, the cylinder block is made from cast-iron, and the cylinder bores are an integral part of the cylinder biock, On this type of engine, the cylinder bores are generally reterred to as having dry Iiners.

The iniet and exhaust valves are each closed by coil springs, and operate in guides pressed into the cylinder head; the valve seat inserts are also pressed inta the cylinder head, and can be renewed separately iIf worn.

The camshaft rotates directly in the cylinder head, is driven by a toothed timing belt, and operates the eight valves via rocker arms. Valve clearances are adjusted by a screwand-locknut arangement, The timing belt aiso crives the coolant pump.

Lubrication is by means of an oll pump. which is driven (Ma a chain and sprocket) off! the right-hand end of the crankshaft. It draws oil through a strainer located in the sump, and then foroes it through an extemally-moumted fiter into galleries in the cylinder block/crankcase. From there, the oll is distributed to the crankshaft (main bearings) and camshaft. The big-end bearings are supplied with oil via interal drilings in the crankshaft, while the camshaft bearings aiso receive a pressurised supply, The camshaft lobes and vaives are lubricated by splash, as are all other engine components.

Throughout  this manual, it  is often necessary to identity the engines not only by their capacity, but also by their engine code which can be found on the left-hand end of the front face of the cylinder block. On engines with an aluminium cylinder bliock, the code is stamped on a plate which is rveted to the block; on engines with a cast-iron cylinder block, the number is stamped on a machined surface on the cylinder block, at the fywheel end. The first part of the engine number gives the engine code — eg KFX (see illustration).

# 2 Compression test –

description and interpretation

1 When engine performance is down, or if misfining occurs which cennot be atiributed to the ignition or fuel systems, a compression test can provide diagnostic clues as to the engine's condition, If the test is performed regularly, it can give wamning of irouble before any other symptoms become apparent.

2 The engine must be fuly warmed-up to normal cperating temperature, the battery must be fully charged, and all the spark plugs must be removed (see Chapter 1A). The aid of an assistant will also be required.

3 Disable and depressurise the fuel system, either by disconnecting the fuel pump wining connector (refer to Chapter 4A) or by identifying and removing the fuel pump fuse from the fusebox, Star the engine, and run it until it cuts out.

4 Disable the ignition system , by disconnecting the LT wiring connector from the ignition HT coil, or ignition coil module, refeming to Chapter 5B for further information. 5 Fit a compression tester to the No 1 cylinder spark plug hole — the type of tester which screws into the plug thread is to be preterred,

6 Have the assistant hold the throttle wide open, and crank the engine on the starter motor; after one or two revalutions,  the compression pressure should build up to a maximum figure, and then stabilise. Record the highest reading obtained.

7 Repeat the test on the remaining cylinders, recording the pressure in each.

8 All cylinders should produce very similar pressures; a difference of more than 2 bars between any two cylinders indicates a fault. Note that the compression should build up quickly in a healthy engine; low compression on the first stroke, followed by graduallyincreasing pressure on successive strokes, indicates wom piston rings. A low compression reading on the first stroke, which does not bulld up duning successive strokes, indicates leaking valves or a biown head gasket (a cracked head could also be the cause). Deposits an the undersides 'of the valve heads can aiso cause low compression. e Although Ciroen  do not  specify exact compression pressures, as & guide, any cylinder pressure of below 10 bars can be considered as less than healthy, Aeter to a Citroen dealer or ather specialist if in doubt as to whether a particular pressure reading is acceptabie

![](images/f01380a757f336850f463f57870e98ac9a0c21f6b617882a35e8477fff135cfe.webp)  
3.4 Insert a 6 mm bolt (arrowed) through the hole in cylinder block flange and into the timing hole in the flywheel .. .

10If the pressure in any cylinder is low, cary out the following test to isolate the cause. Introduce a teaspoonful of clean oil into that cylinder through its spark plug hole, and repeat the test.

11If the addition of oil temporarily improves the compression pressure, this indicates that bore or piston wear is responsible for the pressure loss. No improvement suggests thet leaking or bumt valves, or a blown head gasket, may be to blame.

12 A low reading from two edjacent cylinders is aimost certainly due to the head gasket having blown between them;  the presence of coolant in the engine oil will confirm this.

13 If the compression reading is unusually high, the combustion chambers are probably coated with carbon deposits. If this is the case, the cylinder head should be removed and decarbonised.

14 On completion of the test, reft the spark plugs and reconnect the ignition system.

6Timing belt - general information, removal and refitting

Note: Citroen specilfy the use of an electronic belt tension checking tool (SEEM 4122-7), and vaive rocker contact plate (4533-7.Z.) to comectly set the timing beit tension, The following procedure assumes that tns equipment (or sultabile alternatives) is avalable. Accurate tensioning of the timing beit is essential, and if access to this equipment cannol be obisined,  it is recommended that the work is entrusted to a Citroen dealer or sultably-equlpped garage.

# General information

1 The timing belt drives the camshaft and caolant pump from a toothed sprocket on the right-hand end of the crankshaft. if the belt breaks or slips in service, the pistons are sikely to hit the valve heads, resuling in extensive (and expensive) damage.

2 The timing belt should be renewed at the specified intenvals (see Chapter 1A), or earlier if it is contaminated with oll or if it is at all noisy in operation (a 'scraping' noise due to uneven werer).

3 if the timing belt is being removed, it is a wise precaution to check the condition of the coolant pump at the same time (check for signs of coolant leakage), This may avoid the need to remove the timing belt again at a later stage, should the coolant pump fail.

# Removal

4 Disconnect the battery negative terrminal (refer to Disconnecting the battery in the Reference Section of this manuan.

5 Align the engine assembly/valve timing holes as described in Section 3, and lock both the camshaft sprocket and the flywheel in position. Do not attempt to rotate the engine whilst the locking tools are in position.

6 Remove the liming belt centre and lower covers as described in Section 5.

7 Loosen the timing belt tensioner pulley retaining nut. Allow the pulley to pivot in a clockwise direction, to relieve the tension from the timing beit. Retighten the tensioner pulley retaining nut to secure it in the slackened position.

8If the timing belt is to be re-used, use white paint or similar to mark the direction of rotation on the belt (f markings do not already exist) (see illustration), Slip the belt off the sprockets.

Check the timing beit carefuty for any signs of uneven wear, spliting, or oil contamination. Pay particular aftention to the roots of the teeth. Renew the belit if there is the slightest doubt about its condition. If the engine is undergoing an overhaul, and has covered more than 37 500 miles (60 000 km) with the existing belt fitted, renew the belt as a matter of course, regardless of its apparent condition. The cost of a new belt is nothing when compared to the cost of repairs, should the belt break in service. If signs of oll contamination are found, trace the source of the oll leak, and rectity it. Wash down the engine timing beit area and all related components, to remove all traces of oll.

# Tensioning

14 Fit the sensor head of the electronic belt tensioning measuning equipment to the "front run' of the tining belt, approximately midway between the camahaft and crankshaft sprockets.

15 Siecken the tensioner pulley retaining nut and insert a short length of 8,0 mm square bar into the square hole on the front face of the tensioner pulley (see Tool Tip 1).

16  Using the square bar and a spanner, pivot the tensloner pulley anti-clockwise untlil an initial setting of 44 SEEM units is displayed on the tensioning measuring equipment (see ilustration). Hold the tensioner pulley in that position and retighten the retaining nut.

17 Remove the locking tools from the camshaft sprocket and flywheel, and remove the tension measuring equipment from the belt.

18  Using a sutable socket and extension bar on the crankshaft sprocket boit, rotate the crankshaf through tour complete rotations in a clockwise direction (viewed trom the nghthand end of the engine). Do not at any time rotate the crankshaft anti-clockwise. Refit the locking tool to the flywheel and check that the camshaft sprocket timing hole is aligned.

19 To enable an accurate beit tension final satting to be achieved, all the load exerted on the camshaft lobes through the action of the valve springs and rocker arms must be removed. To do this, Citroen mechanics use a vaive rocker contact plate (special tool 4533-T,Z.) which is simply a steel plate ritted over the rocker arms in place of the cylinder head cover, and secured using the cylinder head cover retaining nuts. Eigh studs and locknuts are titted ta the plate, one jocated directly over the valve stem end of each rocker arm. The studs are then screwed down until they just Iift the rocker arms away from the camshaft lobes and are then secured in that position with the locknuts. This has the effect of removing all the load from the camshaft, alliowing it to move very slighitly as the belt tension is adjusted. If this is not done, the tension reading shown on the beit tension measuning equipment will be inaccurete, If the special tool cannot be obtained, a suitable altemative can be fabricated (see Tool Tip 2).

# 9 Valve clearances - checking and adjustment

Note: The vave clearences must be checked and edjusted anly when the engine is cold.

1 The importance of having the valve clearances corectly adjusted cannot  be overstressed, as they vitally affect the performance of the engine, If the clearances are too big. the engine will be noisy (charactenistic ratting or tapping noises) and engine efficiency will be reduced, as the valves open too late and close too early. A more serious problem arises if the clearances are too small, however, If this is the case, the vaives may not close fully when the engine is hot, resulting in serious damage to the engine (eg, burnt valve seats and/or cylinder head warping/cracking). The clearances are checked and adjusted as follows.

3 The engine can now be tumed using a suitable socket and extension bar fitted to the crankshaft sprocket/pulley balt.

The correct valve clearances are given in the Specifications at the start of this Chapter. The valve locations can be deternined from the position of the manifolds,

# General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the XU series petrol engines. Similar information covering the TU series petrol engines, and the diesel engines will be found in Chapters 2A, 2C and 2D. All procedures concerning engine removal and refitting. and engine block/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

Refer to Vehicle identification in the Reference Section of this manual for detais of enaine code locations.

Most of the operations included in Chapter 2B are based on the assumption that the engine is sti installed in the car. Therefore, f this information is being used during a complete engine overhaul, with the engine already removed, many of the steps included here will not apply.

# XU series engine description

The XU series engine is a well-proven power unit which has been fited to many previous Citroin and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of the in-line four-cylinder type. mounted transversely at the front of the car with the clutch and transmission attached to its left-hand end. The Xsara range is fitted with 1.8 litre (1761cc) and 2.0 litre (1998cc) engines. Both 8and 16-valve versions of the 1.8 litre engine are avalable, whereas all 2.0 itre engines are of 16-valve configuration.

The crankshaft runs in five main bearings. Thrustwashers are fitted to No 2 main bearing cap, to control crankshaft endfioat.

The connecting rods ratate on horzontallysplit bearing shelis at their big-ends. The pistons are attached to the connecting rods by gudgeon pins which are an interference fit in the connecting rod small-end eyes. The aluminium alloy pistons are fitted with three piston rings - two compression rings and an oil control ring.

On 1.8 litre engines, the cylinder block is of the wet-liner' type. The biock is cast in aluminium alloy. and the bores have replaceable cast-iron liners that are located fram the top of the cylinder block. Sealing O rings are fitted at the base of each liner, to orevent the escape of coolant into the sump.

On 2.0 litre engines, the cylinder block is of the conventional 'dry-liner' type. The biock is of cast iron, and no separate bore liners are fitted.

On the 8-vaive engines, the camshaft is driven by a toothed timing belt. and it operates the valves via followers located beneath each cam lobe. The vaive clearances are adjusted by shims, positioned between the foltowers and the tip of the valve stem.

The camshatts on 16-valive engines are also driven by a common toothed timing belt; the front camshaft operates the inlet valves, and the rear camshaft operates the exhaust valves. The vaive clearances are seif-adjusting by means of hydraulic tappets.

Each camshaft runs in bearing caps which are bolted to the top of the cylinder head. The iniet and exhaust vaives are each closed by coil springs, and operate in guides pressed into the cylinder head. Both the valve seats and guides can be renewed separately if wom.

The coolant pump is aiso driven by the timing belt. and is located in the right-hand end of the cylinder biock.

Lubrication is by means of an oil pump which is driven (via a chain and sprocket) off the crankshaft right-hand end. it draws oil through a strainer located in the sump, and then forces it through an externally-mounted fiter into gallries in the cylinder block/crankcase. From there, the oill is distributed to the crankshaft (main bearings) and carshaft. The big-end bearings are supplied with oi via internal drilings in the crankshaft; the camshaft bearings also receive a pressurised supply. The camshaft lobes and valves are lubricated by splash, as are all other engine components. On certain engines, an oil cooler is mounted beneath the oil fiter cartridge, to keep the oil temperature constant under severe operating conditions. The oil cooler is supplied with coolant from the engine cooling system.

Throughout the manual, it is often necessary to identify the engines not only by their cubic capacity, but aiso by their engine code. The engine code, consists of three letters (eg. LFZ. On 1.8 itre engines the code is stamped on a plate attached to the front. left-hand end of the cylinder biock, and on 2.0 litre engines the engine code is stamped directly onto the front face of the cylinder biock, on the machined surface located just to the left of the oil fiter (next to the crankcase vent hose union).

# General information

10 Check the timing belt carefully for any signs of uneven wear, splitting. or oil contamination. Pay particular attention to the roots of the teeth. Renew it if there is the slightest doubt about its condition. If the engine is undergoing an overhaul, and has covered more than 37 500 miles (60 000 km) with the existing beit fitted, renew the belt as a matter of course, regardless of its apparent condition. The cost of a new beit is nathing compared with the cost of repairs, shouild the belt break in service. If signs of oil contamination are found, trace the source of the oil leak and rectity it. # General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the XUD series diesel engines. Similar information covering the DW series diesel engines, and the petrol engines wil be found in Chapters 2A, 28 and 2D. Al procedures conceming engine removal and refiting, and engine block/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

Refer to Vehicle identification in the Reference Section of this manual for detaisof engine code locations.

Most of the operations included in Chapter 2C are based on the assumption that the engine is stillinstalled in the car. Therefore. this information is being used during a complet ege ovea with the ee already removed, many of the steps included here will not apply.

# XUD series engine description

The XUD series engine is a well-proven moder unit which has appeared in many Citroän and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of four-cylinder overhead camshaft design, mounted transversely, with the transmission mounted on the left-hand side.

A toothed timing belt drives the camshaft, fuel injection pump and coolant pump. Followers are fited between the camshaft and valves. Valve clearance adjustment is by means of shims. The camshaft is supported by three bearings machined directly in the cylinder head.

The crankshaft uns in five main bearings of the usual shel type. Endioat is controlled by thrustwashers either side of No 2 main beaing.

The pistons are selected to be of matching weightand inorpoatefuy-foatng gudgeon pins retained by circlips.

The oil pump is chain-driven from the nghthand and of the crankshaft. An oll cooler s ited to all engines.

The design of the turbo engine is the same as the normally-aspirated (non-turbo version.

but components such as the crankshaft, pistons and connecting rods are uprated.It also incorporates oil jets which spray oil anto the undersides af the pistons to keep them cool.

Throughout the manual, itis often necessary to identiy the engines not only by their cubic capacity, but also by their engine code. The engine code. consists of three letters (e DJy). The code is stamped on a plate attached to the front of the cylinder block.

# Compression test

Note: A compression tester specificaly designed for diesel engines must be used for this fest.

1 When engine performance is down, or if misfring occurs which cannot be attributed to the fuel system, a compression test can provide diagnostic clues as to the engine's condition, If the test is performed regularly, t can give warning of trouble before any ather symptoms become apparent.

2 A compression tester specificaly intended for diesel engines must be used, because of the higher pressures involved. The tester is connected to an adapter which screws into the glow plug or injector hole. On these engines, an adapter suitable for use in the injector holes will be required, due to the imited access to the glow plug holes (see iustration). It is ulikely to be worthwhile buyng such atesterfor occasional use but

may be possible to borrow or hire one - if not,   
have the test performed by a garage.   
Unless speci istructions to the contray   
are supplied with the tester, observe the   
following points:   
The battery must be in a good state of charge, the i itermust be can, and the engine should be at nomal operatig temperature.   
All the injectors or glow plugs should be eoved beforetarting the tes removing the injectors, also remove the fame shield washers, othenwise they may be biown out. Refer to Chapters 4B and SC for further information.   
The anti-theft system alectronic engine immodiliser unit wirng connector at the rear of the injection pump must be disconnected.

4 There is no need to hold the accelerator pedal down during the test. because the diesel engine ai inet is not throtted.

5 The compression pressures measured are not so important as the balance between cylinders. Values are given in the Specifications.

6The cause of poor compression is less easy to establish on a diesel angine than on a petrol one. The effect of introducing oilinto the cylinders wet' testing) i not conclusive. because there  ask tat theil willit nhe swirt chamber or in the recess on the piston crown instead of passing to the rings. However the following canbe used rough guide to diagnosis.

7 All cylinders should produce very similar pressures; any difference greater than that specified indicates the existence of a fault. Note that the compression should buld up quickly in a healhy engine; low compression on the first stroke, followed by gradually. increasing pressure on successive strokes. indicates worn piston rings. A low compression reading on the first stroke, which does not build up during successive strokes. indicates leaking vaives or  blown heed gasket (a cracked head could aiso be the cause. Deposits on the undersides of the valve heads can aiso cause low compression. A low reading from two adjacent cylinders is almost certainly due to the head gasket having biown between them; the presence of coolant in the engine o will confirm this.

9 if the compression reading is unusually high. the cylinder head surfaces, valves and pistons are probably coated with carbon deposits. f this is the case, the cylinder head should be removed and decarbonised (see Part F.

# Leakdown test

10 A leakdown test measures the rate at which compressed air fed into the cylinderis lost It is an aeAtiv tO a compressin tes. and in many ways it is better, since the escaping air provides easy identitication of where pressure loss is occuming (piston rings. valves or head gasket).

11 The equipment needed tor leakdown testing is unlikely to be available to the home mechanic. If poor compression is suspected. have the test performed by a suitablyequipped garage.

# Inspection

11 Check the timing belt carefully for any signs of uneven wear, split or ol contamination. Pay particular attention to the roots of the teeth. Renew it if there is the slightest doubt about its condition. If the engine is undergoing an overhaul, and has covered more than 40 000 miles (60 000 km) with the existing belt fitted, renew the belt as a matter of course, regardless of its apparent condition. The cost of a new bet is nothing compared with the cost of repairs, should the belt break in service. If signs of oil contamination are found, trace the source of the ail leak and rectify it. Wash down the engine timing belt area and all related camponents, to remove all traces of oi. Check that the tensioner and ider pulley rotates frely. without any sign of roughness. If necessary. renew as described in Sections 9 and 10 (as applicable

# 12 Valve clearances - checking and adjustment

#

1 The importance of having the valve clearances correctly adjusted cannot be overstressed, as they vitally affect the perfarmance of the engine. Checking should

not be regarded as a routine operation, however. It should only be necessary when the valve gear has become noisy, after engine overhaul, or when trying to trace the cause of power loss. The clearances are checked as follows. The engine must be cold for the check to be accurate.

2 Chock the rear wheeis then jack up the front of the car and support it on axle stands (see Jacking and vehicle support). Remove the right-hand tront roadwheel.

3 From undemeath the front of the car. remove the wheelarch plastic liner, which is secured by various screws and clips under the wheelarch. Release al the fasteners, and remove liner from under the front wing. Where necessary, unclip the coolant hoses from under the wing to improve access to the crankshaft pulley.

4 The engine can now be tumed over using a suitable socket and extension bar fitted to the crankshaft pulley bolt.

6 On a piece of paper, draw the outine of the engine with the cylinders numbered from the fywheel end. Show the position of each valve, together with the specified valve clearance. Above each valve, draw ines for noting (1) the actual clearance and (2) the amount of adjustment required (see illustration).

7 Turm the crankshaft until the inlet valve of No 1 cylinder (nearest the transmission) is fully closed, with the tip of the cam facing directly away from the follower.

8 Using feeler blades, measure the clearance between the base of the cam and the cam follower (see ilustration) Record the clearance on line (1).

9 Repeat the measurement for the other seven valves, turning the crankshaft as necesary so that the cam lobe in question is always facing directly away ftrom the relevant fofiower.

10 Calculate the difference between each measured clearance and the desired value. and record it on line (2). Since the clearance is different far inlet and exhaust vaives - make sure that you are aware which valve you are dealing with. The valve sequence from either end of the engine is:

# Adjustment

12 Remove the camshaft as described in Section 11.

# L

13 Withdraw the first follower and its shim. Be careful that the shim does not fall out of the follower. Clean the shim, and measure its thickness with a micrometer. The shims carry thickness markings, but wear may have reduced the ariginal thickness, so be sure to check.

14 Refer to the clearance recorded for the vaive concerned. If the clearance was more than that specified, the shim thickness must be increased by the difference recorded (2). If the clearance was less than that specified, the thickness of the shim must be decreased by the difference recorded (2).

15 Draw three more lines beneath each valve on the calculation paper, as shown in ilustration 12.6. On line (4) note the measured thickness of the shim, then add or deduct the difference from line (2) to give the final shim thickness required on line (5).

16 Repeat the procedure given in paragraphs 13 to 15 on the remaining valves, keeping each follower identified for position.

17 When reassembling, oil the shim and fit it into the valve retainer, with the size marking face downwards. Oil the fallower, and tower it onto the shim. Do not raise the follower after iting, as the shim may become disiodged.

18 When all the followers are in position, complete with their shims, refit the camshaft as described in Section 11. Recheck the valve ciearances before refiting the cylinder head cover, to make sure they are corect.

# Preparation for refitting

23The mating faces of the cylinder head and cylinder block/crankcase must be perfectly clean before refitting the head. Citron recommend the use of a scouring agent for this purpose, but acceptable results can be achieved by using a hard plastic or wood scraper to remove all traces of gasket and carbon. The same method can be used to clean the piston crowns. Take particular care to avoid scoring or gouging the cylinder head/cylinder block mating surfaces during the cleaning operations, as aluminium alioy is easily damaged. Make sure that the carbon is not aliowed to enter the oil and water passages - this is particularly important for the lubrication system, as carbon could biock the

B oi supply to the engine's components. Using adhesive tape and paper, seal the water, oi and boit holes in the cylinder block/crankcase. To prevent carbon entering the gap between the pistons and bores, smear a little grease in the gap. After cleaning each piston, use a small brush to remove al traces of grease and carbon from the gap, then wipe away the remainder with a clean rag.

If warpage of the cylinder head gasket surface is suspected, use a straight-edge to check it for distortion. Refer to Part F of this Chapter if necessary.

# General information and precautions

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures far the DW series diesei engines, Similar information covering the XUD series diesel engines, and the petrol engines wil be found in Chapters 2A, 28 and 2C. Al procedures conceming engine removal and refitting, and engine biock/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in'Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

Refer to Vehicle identification in the Reference Section of this manual for details of engine code locations.

Most of the operations included in Chapter 2D are based on the assumption that the engine is stillinstaled in the car. Therefore, if this information is being used during a complete engine overhaul, with the engine aready removed, many of the steps included here wil not apply.

# DW series engine description

The DW series engine is a relatively new power unit based on the well-proven XUD series engine which has appeared in many Ciron and Peugeot vehicles. The 1.9 itre (Dw8) engine is virtually identical to the 1. itre XUD unit apart from revisions to the cylinder head cover and fuel system components. The 2.0 itre (DWTD) engine i very similar to the XUD engine in terms of the cylinder block components, but the remainder of the engine has been compietely redesigned. Both engines are of four-cylinder single overhead camshaft design, mounted transversely, with the transmission mounted on the left-hand side.

On the 1.9 litre engine, a toothed timing belt drives the camshaft, fuel injection pump and coolant pump. Followers are fitted between the camshaft and vaives, with valve clearance adjustment being by means of shims, The camshaft is supported by three bearings machined directly in the cylinder head.

On the 2.0 Iitre engine, a toothed timing belt drives the camshaft, high pressure fuel pump and coolant pump. The camshaft operates the inlet and exhaust valves via rocker arms which are supported at their pivot ends ty hydraulic self-adjusting tappets. The camshaft is supported by six bearings machined directly in the cylinder head and camshaft bearing housing

The crankshaft runs in five main bearings of the usual shel type. Endfoat is controled by thrustwashers either side of No 2 main bearing.

The pistons are selected to be of matching weight, and ncorporate fuly-foating gudgean pins retained by circlips.

The oil pump is chain-driven fram the ightnand end of the crankshaft and an oil cooler i fited to al engines.

Throughout the manual, it is often necessary to identify the engines not only by their cubic capacity, but aiso by their engine code. The engine code, consists of three letters (eg, DWB). The code is stamped on a plate attached to the front of the cylinder block.

# Repair operations – precaution

The 2.0 itre engine is a complex unit with numerous accessories and ancillary components. The design of the engine compartment is such that every conceivable space has been utilised, and access to virtually all of the engine components is extremely limited. In many cases, ancillary components will have to be removed, or moved to one side, and wiring. pipes and hoses will have to be disconnected or removed from various cable clips and support brackets.

When working on this engine, read through the entire procedure first, look at the car and engine at the same time, and establish whether you have the necessary tools, equipment, skill and patience to proceed. Allow considerable time for any operation, and be prepared for the unexpected. Any major work on this engines is not for the fainthearted!

Because of the limited access, many of the 2.0 itre engine photographs appearing in this Chapter were, by necessity, taken with the engine removed from the vehicle.

Warning: It is essential to observe strict precautions when working on the fuel system components of the 2.0 litre

engine, particularty the high pressure side of the system. Before carrying out any engine operations that entail working on, or near, any part of the fuel system, refer to the special information given in Chapter 4C, Section 2.

# Compression and leakdown tests - description and interpretation

# Compression test

Note: A compression tester specifically designed for diesel engines must be used for this test.

3 Unless specific instructions to the contrary are Supplied with the tester, observe the following points:

aThe battery must be in a good state of charge, the air fiter must be clean, and the engine should be at normal operating temperature.   
Al the glow plugs should be removed as described in Chapter 5C before starting the test.   
c On 1.9 litre engines the ant-theft system ciectronic engine immobliser unit wiring connector at the rear of the injection pump must be disconnected.   
d On 2.0 titre engines the wining connector on the engine management system ECU (located in the plastic box behind the battery) must be disconnected.

1 When engine pertormance is down, or if misfiring occurs which cannot be attributed to the tuel system, a compression test can provide diagnostic clues as to the engine's condition. If the test is performed regularly, it can give warning of trouble before any other symptoms become apparent.

мм

2 A compression tester specificaly intended for diesel engines must be used, because of the higher pressures invaived. The tester is connected to an adapter which screws into the glow plug or injector hole. On these engines, an adapter suitable for use in the gliow plug holes wil be required, so as not to disturb the fuel system components. It is uniikely to be worthwhile buying such a tester for occasional use, but it may be possible to borrow or hire one - if not. have the test performed by a garage.

4 The compression pressures measured are not so important as the balance between cylinders. Vaiues are given in the Specifications. 5 The cause of poor compression is less easy to establish on a diesel engine than on a petral one. The effect of introducing oil into the cylinders ('wet' testing) is not conclusive. because there is a risk that the oil wil sit n the swirl chamber or in the recess on the piston crown instead of passing to the rings. However, the following can be used as a rough guide to diagnosis.

6 All cylinders should produce very similar pressures; any difference greater than that specified indicates the existence of a fault. Note that the compression should build up quickly in a healthy engine; low compression on the first stroke, followed by graduallyincreasing pressure on successive strokes. indicates worn piston rings. A low compression reading on the first stroke, which does not build up during successive strokes, indicates leaking valves or a blown head gasket (a cracked head could also be the cause). Deposits on the undersides of the valve heads can also cause low compression. 7 A low reading from two adjacent cylinders is aimost certainly due to the head gasket having biown between them; the presence of coolant in the engine oil will contirm this.

8 if the compression reading is unusually high, the cylinder head surfaces, valves and pistons are probably coated with carbon deposits. If this is the case, the cylinder head should be removed and decarbonised (see Part F.

# Leakdown test

9 A leakdown test measures the rate at which compressed air fed into the cylinder is lost. It is an alternative to a compression test, and in many ways it is better, since the escaping air provides easy identification of where pressure loss is occuming (piston rings, valves or head gasket).

10 The equipment needed for leakdown testing is unlikely to be availabie to the home mechanic, If poor compression is suspected. have the test performed by a suitablyequipped garage.

The Hi type ful system used on these engines does not have a conventional diesel injection pump. but instead uses a high pressure fuel pump that does not have to be timed. The alignment of the fuel pump sprocket (and hence the fuel pump itself) with respect to crankshaft and camshaft position, is therefore irrelevant.

# Timing belt (1.9 litre engines) removal, inspection, refiting and tensioning

Note: Citron specify the use of an electronic belt tension checking tool (SEEM 4122-7) to correctly set the timing belt tension. The

S 3

falowing procedure assumes that this equipment (or suitable alternative equipment calibrated to display belt tension in SEEM units) is available. Accurate tensioning of the timing belt is essential, and if the electronic equipment is not avalable, it is recommended that the work is entrusted to a Citron dealer or sutably-equipped garage.

# General

1 The timing belt drives the camshaft, injection pump, and coolant pump from a toothed sprocket on the right-hand end of the crankshaft. The beit also drives the brake vacuum pump indirectly via the rear ("flywheel) end of the camshaft. If the belt breaks or slips in service, the pistons are likely to hit the valve heads, resulting in expensive damage.

2 The timing belt should be renewed at the specified intervais, or earlier if it is contaminated with oil, or at all noisy in aperation (a 'scraping' noise due to uneven wear).

3 if the timing belt is being removed, it is a wise precaution to check the condition of the coolant pump at the same time (check for signs of coolant leakage. This may avoid the need to remove the timing beit again at a later stage, should the coolant pump fail.

4 Remove the upper, intermediate and lower timing belt covers as described in Section 6.

5 Align the engine assembly/valve timing holes as described in Section 3, and lock the camshaft sprocket hub, injection pump hub, and flywheel in position. Do not attempt to rotate the engine whist the pins are in position.

6 Remove the right-hand engine mounting as described in Section 18.

7 Siacken the three bolts securing the camshaft sprocket to the sprocket hub (see illustration.

Similarly slacken the three boits securing the injection pump sprocket to the pump hub. Loosen the timing belt tensioner pulley retaining bolt. Allow the pulley to pivot in a clockwise direction, to relieve the tension from the timing balt. Retighten the tensioner pulley retaining bolt to secure it in the slackened position.

10 if the timing belt is to be re-used, use white paint or chalk to mark the direction of rotation on the belt (of markings do not aready exist), then slip the belt off the sprockets. Note that the crankshaft must not be rotated whist the belt is removed.

with the existing belt fitted, renew the belt as a matter of course, regardless of its apparent condition. The cost of a new belt is nothing compared with the cost of repairs, should the belt break in service. If signs of oil contamination are found, trace the source of the oil leak and rectify it. Wash down the engine timing belt area and all related components, to remove all traces of ail. Check that the tensioner pulley and idier roller rotate freely, without any sign of roughness. If necessary, renew as described in Section 9.

# Refitting

14 Locate the timing belt on the crankshaft sprocket, making sure that, where applicabie. the direction of rotation arrow is facing the correct way.

6 Remove the locking tool from the camshaft sprocket hub. Siacken the sprocket hub retaining boit, and the three sprocket-tohub retaining boits. To prevent the camshaft rotating as the boits are slackened, a sprocket holding tool will be required. In the absence of the special Citroän tool, an acceptable substitute can be fabricated at home (see Tool Tip 1. Do not attempt to use the engine assembly/valve timing locking tool to prevent the sprocket from rotating whilst the bolt is slackened.

7 Remove the sprocket hub retaining boit and washer, and slide the sprocket and hub off the end of the camshaft. If the Woodruff key is a loose fit in the camshaft, remove it for safekeeping. Examine the camshaft oil seal for signs of oil leakage and, if necessary, renew it as described in Section 16.

8 If necessary, the sprockat can be separated trom the hub after removing the three retaining boits.

Clean the camshaft sprocket thoroughly. and renew it if there are any signs of wear, damage or cracks.

1 The importance of having the valve clearances correctly adjusted cannot be overstressed, as they vitally aftect the performance of the engine. Checking should not be regarded as a routine operation, however. It should only be necessary when the valive gear has become noisy, after engine overhaul, or when trying to trace the cause of power loss. The clearances are checked as foliows. The engine must be cold for the check to be accurate.

# Preparation for refitting

18The mating faces of the cylinder head and cylinder biock/crankcase must be perfectly clean before refitting the head. Citron recommend the use of a scouring agent for this purpose, but acceptable resuits can be achieved by using a hard plastic or wood scraper to remove all traces of gasket and carbon. The same method can be used to clean the piston crowns. Take particular care to avoid scoring or gouging the cylinder head/cylinder block mating surfaces during the cleaning operatiors, as aluminium alloy is easily damaged. Make sure that the carbon is not allowed to enter the oll and water passages - this is particularly important for the lubrication system, as carbon could biock the oil supply to the engine's components. Using adhesive tape and paper, seal the water, oil and bolt holes in the cylinder block/crankcase. To prevent carbon entering the gap between the pistons and bores. smear a littie grease in the gap. After cieaning each piston, use a small brush to remove all traces of grease and carbon from the gap. then wipe away the remainder with a clean rag
