# 1General information

Included in this Part of Chapter 2 are details of removing the engine/transmission from the car and general overthaul procedures for the cylinder head, cylinder biock/crankcase and all other engine internal components.

The information given ranges from advice concering preparation for an averhaul and the purchase of replacement parts, to detailed step-by-step procedures covering removal, inspection, renovation and refitting of engine internal components.

After Section 6, all instructions are based on the assumption that the engine has been removed from the car. For information conceming in-car engine repair, as wel as the removal and refitting of those external companents necessary for full overhaul, refer to Part A or B of this Chapter (as applicabie) and to Section 6. Ignore any preliminary dismanting operations described in Part A or B that are no longer relevant once the engine has been removed from the car.

Apart trom torque wrench settings, which are given at the beginning of Part A or B (as applicable), all specifications relating to engine overhaul are at the beginning of this Part of Chapter 2.

# Engine overhaul - general information

It is not always easy to determine when, or i, an engine should be compietely overhauled, as a number of factors must be considered.

High mileage is not necessarily an indication that an overnaul is needed, while low mileage does nat preclude the need for an overhaul, Frequency of servicing is probably the most important consideration, An engine which has had regular and frequent oil and fiter changes, as well as other required maintenance, shouid give many thousands of miles of reliable service. Conversely. neglected engine may require an overhau! very early in its Iife.

Excessive oi consumption is an indication that piston rings, vaive seals and/or valve guides are in need of attention. Make sure that oil leaks are not responsibie before deciding that the rings and/or guides are worn. Perform a compression test. as described in Part A of this Chapter. to determine the likely cause of the problem.

Check the ail pressure with a gauge fitted in place of the oil pressure switch, and compare it with that specified in Part A or B of this Chapter. If it is extremely low, the main and big-end bearings, and/or the oil pump, are probably wom out.

Loss of power, rough running, knocking or metallic engine noises, excessive valve gear noise, and high fuel consumption may also point to the need for an overhaul, especially if they are al present at the same time. If a complete service does not remedy the situation, major mechanical work is the only solution.

An engine overthaul invoives restoring all internal parts to the specification of a new engine, During an overhaul, the cyinder liners (where appicabiej, the pistons and the piston rings are renewed. New main and big-end bearings are generally fitted; if necessary, the crankshaft may be reground to restore the journais. The vaives are aiso serviced as well. since they are usually in less-than-perfect condition at this point. The end result should be an as-new engine that wil give many trouble-free miles.

Note: Critical cooling system components such as the hoses, thermostat and coclant pump should be renewed when an engine is overhauled. The radiator should be checked

2E•4 Petrol engine removal and overhaul procedures carefuly, to ensure that it is not clogged or e Asois a good d toe the pump whenever the engine is overhauled.

Before beginning the engine overmaul, read through the entire procedure, to famiiarise yourseif with the scope and requirements of the Oveauling anengine is nat dificut  you fllw carefuly al of the instructions, have the necessary toois and equipment, and pay ciose attention to all specifications. It can, however, be time-consuming. Plan on the car being off the road for a minimum of two weeks. especially if parts must be taken to an engineering works for repalr or reconditioning. Check on the availabityof parts and make sure that any necessary special tools and equipment are obtained in advance. Most work can be done with typical hand tools, athough a number of precision measuring tools are required forinspecting parts to deterine i they must be renewed. Often the enginearing works will handie the inspection of parts and offer advice conceming reconditioning and renewal.

Always wait until the engine has been completely dismantied, and until all components (especially the cylinder block/crankcase and the crankshaft have been inspected, before deciding what service and repair operations must be performed by an engineering works. The condition of these components will be the major factor to consider when determining whether to overhaul the ariginal engine, or to buy a reconditianed unit. Do not, therefore. purchase parts or have overhaul work done on other components until they have been thoroughly inspected. As a general rule, time is the primary cost of an overhaul, so it does not pay to fit wom or sub-standard parts.

As a final note, to ensure maximum life and minimurn trouble from a reconditioned engine. everything must be assemnbled with care, in a spotiessly-clean environment.

# Engine/transmission removal - methods and precautions

If you have decided that the engine must be removed for overhaul or major repair work. several preliminary steps should be taken.

Locating a suitable place to work is extremely important. Adequate work space. along with storage space for the car, will be neded. I a workshop or garage is not available, at the very least, a flat, level, clean work surface is required.

Cleaning the engine compartment and engine/transmission before beginning the removal procedure wil help keep tools clean and organised.

An engine hoist willalso be necessary. Make sure the equipment is rated in excess of the combined weight of the engine and transmission. Safety is of primary importance, considering the potentiai hazards invoived in sfting the engine/transmission out of the car.

If this is the frst time you have removed an engine, an assistant should ideally be available. Advice and aid trom someone more experienced would aiso be heipful. There are many instances when one person cannot simultaneously perform allof the operations required when liting the engine out of the vehicle.

Plian the operation ahead of time. Before starting work, arrange for the hire of or obtain allof the toois and equipment you willneed. Some of the equipment necessary to perfo engine/transmission removal and installation safely in addition to an engine hoist) is as follows: a heavy duty trolley jack, compiete sets of spanners and sockets as described at the rear of this manual, wooden blocks, and plenty of rags and cleaning solvent for mopping up spiled oil, coolant and fuel if the hoist must be hired, make sure that you arrange for it in advance, and perform alof the aperations possible without t beforehand. This wil save you money and time.

Plan for the car to be out of use for quite a while. An enginering works will be required to perform some of the work which the do-ityourselfer cannot accomplish without special equipment. These places often have a busy schedule, so it would be a good idea to consult them before removing the engine, in order to accurately estimate the amount of time required to rebuid or repair components that may need work.

During the engine removal procedure,  is advisable to make notes of the locations of all brackets, cable ties, earthing points, etc, as well as how the wiring hamnesses, hoses and electrical connections are attached and routed around the engine and engine compartment. An effective way of doing thisis to take a series of photographs of the various companents before they are disconnected or removed. A simple inexpensive disposable camera is ideal for this and the resulting photographs wil prove invaluable when the engine is refitted.

Always be extremely careful when removing and refitting the engine/transmisaion, Serious injury can result from careless actions. Plan ahead and take your time, and a job of this nature, although major, can be accomplished successfully.

Note: The engine can be removed from the car only as a complete unit with the transmission; the two are then separated for overhaul.

1f the valves are in satistactory condition, they should be ground (lapped) into their respective seats, to ensure a smooth, gastight seal If the seat is onty lightly pitted, or if it has been re-cut, fine grinding compound only should be used to praduce the required finish. 14Smear a trace of (the appropriate grade of valve-grinding compound on the seat face. and press a suction grinding tool onto the valve head (see illustration). 15 If coarse grinding compound is being used, work only until a dult, matt even surface is produced on both the valve seat and the vaive, then wipe aff the used compound, and repeat the process with fine compound. When a smooth unbroken ring of ight grey matt finish is produced on both the valve and seat. the grinding operation is complete. Do not grind-in the vaives any further than absolutely necessary, or the seat willbe prematurely sunk into the cylinder head.

# Cast-iron cylinder block

13Visualy check the castings for cracks and corrasion. Look for stripped threads in the threaded holes. It defects are found, have them reaired if cossible, or renew the assembly.

14Check each cylinder bore for scuffing and scoring. Check for signs of a wear ridge at the top of the cylinder, indicating that the bore is excessively womn.

# Aluminium cylinder block with wet liners

18Remove the liner clamps (where used), then use a hard wood drift to tap out each liner from the inside of the cylinder block. When all the liners are released, tip the cylinder block/crankcase on its side and remove each liner from the top of the biock. As each liner is removed, stick masking tape on its left-hand (transmission side) face, and write the cylinder number on the tape. No 1 cylinder is at the transmission (flywheel/ driveplate) end of the engine. Remove the Oring from the base of each liner, and discard (see illustrationsj.

19Check each cylinder liner for scuffing and scoring. Check for signs of a wear ridge at the top of the liner, indicating that the bore is excessively worn.

20 If the necessary measuring equipment is available, measure the bore diameter of each cylinder liner at the top just under the wear ridge). centre, and bottom of the cylinder bore, paraliel to the crankshaft axis.

2 Next, measure the bore diameter at the same three locations, at right-angies to the crankshaft axis. Compare the resuits with the figures given in the Specifications.

2Repeat the procedure for the remaining cvlinder liners.

23 if the liner wear exceeds-the permitted tolerances at any point, or if the cylinder liner walls are badly scored or scuffed. then renewal of the relevant liner assembly wil be necessary. If there is any doubt about the condition of the cylinder bores, seek the advice of an engine reconditioning specialist or Citroen dealer.

24 It renewal is necessary, new liners, complete with pistons and piston rings, can be purchased fror a Citron dealer. Note that it is not possible to buy liners individually they are supplied only as a matched assembly complete with piston and rings.

25 To allow for manufacturing tolerances, pistons and liners are separated into three size groups. The size group of each piston is indicated by a letter (A, B or C) stamped onto its crown, and the size group of each liner is indicated by a series of 1 to 3 notches on the upper lip of the liner, a singe notch for group A, two notches for group B, and three notches for group C. Ensure that each piston and its respective liner are both of the same size group. It is permissible to have different size group piston and liner assemblies fited to the same engine, but never fit a piston of one size group to a liner in a different group. On some later engine, pistons and iners are manufactured in only one size group.

26 Prior to instaling the liners, thoroughly clean the liner mating surfaces in the cylinder block, and use fine abrasive paper to polish away any burs or sharp edges which might damage the liner O-rings. Clean the iners and wipe dry, then fit a new O-ring to the base of each liner. To aid installation, apply a smear of oil to each O-ring and to the base of the iner. 27 itf the original liners are being refitted, use the marks made on removal to ensure that each is refitted the correct way round, and is inserted into its original bore. Insert each liner into the cylinder block, taking care not to damage the O-ring. and press it home as far as possible by hand. Using a hammer and a block of wood, tap each liner lightly but fully onto its locating shoulder. Wipe clean, ther lightly oil al exposed liner surfaces, to prevent rusting.

2 With al four liners corectily instaled, use a dial gauge (or a straight-edge and feeler blade) to check that the protrusion of each liner above the upper surface of the cylinder biock is within the limits given in the Specifications. The maximum ditference between any two liners must not be exceeded.

29 if new liners are being fitted, it is permissible to interchange them to bring the

diterence in _protrusion within limits. Remember to keep each piston with its respective iner.

30 if liner protrusion cannot be brought within limits, seek the advice of an engine reconditioning specialist or Citroen dealer before proceeding with the engine rebuld.

# 13 Piston/connecting rod assembly - inspection

вЩ

1 Before the inspection process can begin, the piston/connecting rod assemblies must be cleaned, and the original piston rings removed from the pistons.

2 Carefully expand the old rings over the top of the pistons. The use of two or three old feler blades will be hetpful in preventing the rings dropping into empty grooves (see Illustration). Be careful not to scratch the piston with the ends of the ring. The rings are britte, and wil shap i they are spread too far. They are aiso very sharp - protect your hands and fingers. Note that the third ring incorporates an expander. Always remove the rings from the top of the piston. Keep each set of ing with i i he old ingare to e re-used.

3 Scrape away all traces of carbon from the top af the piston. A hand-heid wire brush (or a piece of fne emery cloth) can be used, ance the majority of the deposits have been scraped away.

4 Remove the carbon from the ning grooves in the piston, using an old ring. Break the ring in half to do this (be careful not to cut your fingers - piston rings are sharp). Be careful to remove only the carton deposits - do not remove any metal, and do not nick or scratch the sides of the ring grooves.

5 Once the deposits have been removed, clean the piston/connecting rod assembly with paraffin or a suitable soivent, and dry thoroughly. Make sure that the oil retum holes in the ning grooves are clear.

6 If the pistons and cylinder bores are not damaged or worn excessively, and if the cylinder black does not need to be rebored, the original pistons can be refitted. Normal piston wear shows up as even vertical wear on the piston thrust surfaces, and slight looseness of the top ring in its groove. New piston rings should always be used when the engine is reassembled.

7 Carefully inspect each piston for cracks around the skirt, around the gudgeon pin holes, and at the piston ring 'lands' (petween the ring grooves).

6 Look for scoring and scuffing on the piston skirt, hoies in the piston crown, and burned areas at the edge of the crown. If the skirt is scored or scuffed, the engine may have been suffering from overheating, and/or abnormal combustion which caused excessively high operating temperatures. The cooling and lubrication systems should be checked thoroughly. Scorch marks on the sides of the pistons show that blow-by has occurred. A hole in the piston crown, or burned areas at the edge of the piston crown, indicates that abnormal combustion (pre-ignition, knocking. or detonation) has been occurring. If any of the above probiems exist, the causes must be investigated and corrected, or the damage wil occur again.

Corrosion of the piston, in the form of pitting, indicates that coolant has been leaking into the combustion chamber and/or the crankcase. Again, the cause must be corrected, or the problern may persist in the rebuilt engine.

10 On aluminium-block engines with wet liners, it is nat possible to renew the pistons separately: pistons are only supplied with piston rings and a liner, as a part of a matched assembly (see Section 12). On iron-biock engines, pistons can be purchased from a Citroen dealer.

11Examine each connecting rod carefully for signs of damage, such as cracks around the big-end and small-end bearings. Check that the rod is not bent or distorted. Damage is highly unlikely, unless the engine has been seized or badly overheated. Detailed checking of the connecting rod assernbly can anly be carried out by an engine specialist or Citron dealer with the necessary equipment.

12 On XU series engines, the big-end cap nuts and bolts must be renewed as a complete set prior to refitting. This shouid be done after the big-end bearing running clearance check has been carried out (see Section 1 The bolts can be simply tapped out of the connecting rods and new baits titted in the same way.

13 On all engines, the gudgeon pins are an interference fit in the connecting rod smallend bearing Therefore, piston and/or connecting rod renewal should be entrusted to an engine repair specialist who wil have the necessary tooling to remove and install the gudgeon pins.

# 14 Crankshaft – inspection

# Checking crankshaft endfloat

1 If the crankshaft endtfoat is to be checked, this must be done when the crankshaft is stil installed in the cylinder block/crankcase, but is free to move (see Section 11).

2 Check the endfioat using a disl gauge in contact with the end of the crankshaft. Push the crankshaft fuly one way, and then zero the gauge. Push the crankshaft fuly the other way, and check the endfioat. The resut can be compared with the specified amount. and will give an indication as to whether new thrustwashers are required (see illustration).

3 If a dial gauge is not avaiable, feeler biades can be used. First push the crankshaft fully towards the flywheel end of the engine, then use feeler biades to measure the gap between the web of No 2 crankpin and the thrustwasher (see ilustration).

# Inspection

4 Clean the crankshaft using paraffin or a suitabie solvent, and dry it, preferably with compressed air f available. Be sure to clean the oil holes with a pipe cleaner or similar probe, to ensure that they are not obstructed.

# Warning: Wear eye protection when using compressed air.

5 Check the main and big-end bearing jourals for uneven wear, scoring, piting and cracking

6 Big-end bearing wear is accompanied by distinct metalic knocking when the engine is running (particularly noticeable when the engine is puling from low speed and some loss of oil pressure.

7 Main bearing wear is accompanied by severe engine vibration and rumble - getting progressively worse as engine speed increases - and again by loss of ol pressure. a Check the bearing journal for roughness by running a finger lightly over the bearing surface. Any roughness (which will be accompanied by obvious bearing wear indicates that the crankshaft requires rearinding (where possibie) or renewal.

if the crankshaft has been reground, check for burrs around the crankshaft oil holes the holes are usually chamfered, so burrs should not be a problem unless regrinding has been carried out carelessly. Remove any burrs with a fine file or scraper, and thoroughly clean the ail holes as described previously.

10 Using a micrometer, measure the diameter of the main and big-end bearing journals, and compare the results with the Specifications (see Illustration). By measuring the diameter at a number of points around each journal's circumference, you will be able to determine whether or not the journal is out-of-round.Take the measurement at each end of the journal, near the webs, to determine if the journal is tapered. Compare the results obtained with those given in the Specifications. Where no specified joumal diameters are quoted, seek the advice of a Citron dealer.

11 Check the ail seal contact surfaces at each end of the crankshaft for wear and damage. If the seal has worn a deep groove in the surface of the crankshaft, consult an engine overhaul specialist; repair may be possible, but otherwise a new crankshaft wil be required.

# 15 Main and big-end bearingsinspection

1Even though the main and big-end bearings should be renewed during the engine overhaul, the old bearings should be retained for close examination, as they may reveal valuable information about the condition of the engine. The bearing sheils are graded by thickness, the grade of each shell being indicated by the colour code, or size identification, marked on it.

2 Bearing fallure can occur due to lack of lubrication, the presence of dirt or other foreign particies, overioading the engine, or corrosion (see ilustration). Regardless of the cause of bearing failure, the cause must be carrected (where applicable) before the engine is reassembled. to prevent it from happening again.

3 When examining the bearing shelis, remove them from the cylinder block/crankcase, the main bearing ladder/caps (as appropriate), the connecting rods and the connecting rod bigend bearing caps. Lay them aut on a clean surface in the same general position as their location in the engine. This wil enable you to match any bearing probiems with the corresponding crankshaft journal. Do not touch any shell's bearing surface with your fingers while checking it, or the delicate surface may be scratched.

4 Dirt and other foreign matter gets into the engine in a variety of ways. It may be left in the engine during assembly, or it may pass through fiters or the crankcase ventilation

м

system. It may get into the oi, and from there into the bearings. Metal chips from machining operations and nornal engine wear are often present. Abrasives are sometimes left in engine components after reconditioning. especially when parts are not thoroughly cleaned using the proper cleaning methods. Whatever the source, these foreign objects often end up embedded in the soft bearing material, and are easily recognised. Large particles will not embed in the bearing, and will score or gouge the bearing and journal. The best prevention for this cause of bearing tailure is to ciean all parts thoroughly, and keep everything spotiessly-clean during engine assembly. Frequent and regular engine oil and fiter changes are also recommended. 5 Lack of lubrication (or lubrication breakdown has a number of interrelated causes. Excessive heat (which thins the oil. overlcading (which squeezes the oil from the bearing face) and ol leakage (from excessive bearing clearances, worn ol pump or high engine speeds all contribute to lubrication breakdown, Biocked oil passages which usually are the result of misaligned ol holes in a bearing shell, will also aill-starve a bearing. and destroy it. When lack of lubrication is the cause of bearing failure, the bearing matenal is wiped or extruded trom th steal backing of the bearing. Temperaturet may increase to the point where the ste backing tumns blue from overheating.

6 Driving habits can have a definite effect on bearing life. Full-throttie, low-speed cperation (tabouring the engine) puts very high loads on bearings, tending to squeeze out the oil fim. These loads cause the bearings to flex, which produces fine cracks in the bearing face (fatigue failure). Eventually, the bearing material wiloosen in pieces, and tear away from the steel backing.

7Short-distance driving leads to corrosion of bearings, because insufficient engine heat is produced to drive off the condensed water and corrosive gases. These products collect in the engine of, forming acid and sludge. As the oil is carried to the engine bearings, the acid attacks and corrodes the bearing material.

8 Incorect bearing instalation during engine assembly wili lead to bearing failure as well. Tight-fiting bearings leave insufficient bearing running clearance, and will result in oil starvation. Dirt or foreign particles trapped behind a bearing shel result in high spots on the bearina, which lead to failure.

9 Do not touch any shel's bearing surface with your fingers during reassembly; there is a risk of scratching the delicate surface, or of depositing particies of dit on it.

10 As mentioned at the beginning of this Section, the bearing shelfs should be renewed as a matter of course during engine overhaul: to do otherwise is false economy. Refer to Section 18 for details of bearing shel selection.

# General information

Incuded in this Part of Chapter 2 are detais of removing the engine/transmission from the car and general overhaul procedures for the cylinder head, cylinder block/crankcase and llotherengine interal components.

The information given ranges from advice conceming preparation far an overhaul and the purchase of replacement parts, to detailed step-by-step procedures covering removal isection, raion and efting ofee internal components.

After Section 5, all instructions are based on the assumption that the engine has been removed from the car. For information concering in-car engine repair, as well as the remaval and refitting of those external components necessary for full overhaul, refer to Part C or D of this Chapter (as appicabe and to Section 7. Ignore any preliminary dismanting operations described in Part or D that are no longer relevant once the engine has been removed from the car.

Apart from torque wrench settings, which are given at the beginning of Part or  (as applicable), all specifications relating to ninevru are at the beiningof this Part of Chapter 2.

# Engine overhaul - general information

it is not always easy to determine when, or an engine should be completely overhauled, as a number of factors must be considered.

High mileage is not necessanily an indication that an overhaul is needed, while low meage does not preclude the need for an verau.Frequency of servicing is probably the most important consideration. An engine which has had regular and frequent oi and fiter changes, as wel as ather required maintenance, should give many thousands of milas of reliable service. Conversely, a neglected engine may require an overhaul very early in its ite.

Excessive ol consumption is an indication that piston rings, vaive seals and/or valve guides are in ned of attention. Make sure that of leaks are not responsible before deciding that the rings and/or guides are worn. Perform a compression or leakdown test. as described in Part C ar D of this Chapter, to determine the likely cause of the probiem.

Check the ol presure with a gaugefited in place of the oi pressure switch. and compare it that specified it is extremaly lw, the main and big-end bearings and/or the oil pump are probably wom out.

Loss ofpower, rough running, knocking or metalic engine noises, excessive valve gear noise, and high fuel consumption may also point to the need for an overaul, especial f they are all present at the same time  a complete service does not remedy the situation, major mechanical work is the only solution.

An engine overhaul invoives restoring all internal parts to the specification of a new engine During an ovemaul, the cylinder bores re rebored (where necessary), and the pistons and the piston rings are renewed. New main and big-end bearings are generally fitted: if necessary. the crankshaft may be reground, to restore the joumals. The valves are also serviced as well since they are usually in less-than-perfect condition at this point. The end result should be an as-new engine that wilgive many trouble-free miles.

Note: Critical coaling system components such as the hoses, thermostat and coolant pump should be renewed when an engine is overhauled. The radiator should be checked carefuly, to ensure that iis not clogged or leaking Also, it is a good idea to renew the o pump whenever the engine is overhauled.

Before beginning the engine overhaul, read through the entire procedure, to familarise yoursell with the scope and requirements of the jo Overauling an engne i not dicul you follow caretuly al of the instructions, have the necessary toos and equipment, and pay closeattinto al specificatios.It can, however, be time-consuming. Plan on the car being of the road for a minimum of two weeks, epecialy if parts must be taken to an ngieering works for repa or reconditoig Check on the availability of parts and make sure that any necessary special toois and equipment are obtained in advance. Most work can be done with typical hand toois. aithough a number of precision measuring toois are required for inspecting parts to determine it they must be renewed. Often the engineering works wil handle the inspection of parts and offer advice concerning reconditioning and renewal.

Always wait until the engine has been completely dismantied, and unti al components (especialy the cylinder block/crankcase and the crankshaft) have ben inspected, before deciding what service and repar operations must be performed by an engineering works. The condition of these components will be the major factor to consider when determining whether to overhaul the original engine, or to buy a reconditioned unit. Do not. therefore, purchase parts or have overhaul work done on other components until they have been thoroughly ispected. As a generaule e is the primary cost of an overtaul so it does not pay to fit wom or sub-standard parts.

As a final note, to ensure maximum ife and minimum troubie from a reconditioaned engine, everything must be asembled with care. in a spotiessly-clean environment.

# Engine/transmission removalmethods and precautions

If ou have decided that the engine must be removed for veral o major repa wrk. severalprelminary steps should betaken.

Locating a suitable place to work is extremely important. Adequate work space. along with storage space for the car, wil be needed.   workshap or garage is not availabie, at the very least, a flat, level, ciean work surface is required.

Cleaning the engine compartment and engine/transmission before beginning the removal procedure willhelp keep toois clean and organised.

An engine hoist will also be necessary. Make sure the equipment is rated in excess of the combined weight of the engine and transmission. Safety is of primary importance. considering the potential hazards involved in ifting the engine/transmission cut of the car.

If this is the first time you have removed an engine, an assistant should idealy be available. Advice and aid from someone more experienced would aiso be helpful. There re many instances when one person cannot simutaneously perform allof the operations required when iting the engine out of the vehicle.

Pian the operation ahead of time. Before sng wrkra there of o all of the tools and equipment you wil need. Some of the equipment necessary to perfor engine/transmission remaval and installation safely (in addition to an engine hoist) is as follows: a heavy duty tralley jack, complete sets of spanners and sockets as described at the rear of this manual, wooden blocks, and plenty of rags and cleaning solvent tor mopping up spilled oil coolant and fuel if the hoist must be hired, make sure that you arang for tn advance and pertom a the operations possible without it beforeand. This will save you money and time.

Plan for the ca to be cut of use for quite a while. An engineering works will be required to perfom some of the work which the do-it yourselfer cannot accomplish without special equipment. These places often have a busy schedule, so it would be a good idea to consult them before removing the engine, n order to accurately estimate the amount of time required to rebuld or repar components that may need work.

During the engine removal procedure, it is advisable to make notes of the locations of all brackets, cabletes,earing pointsecas well as how the wiring harnesses, hoses and electrical connections are attached and routed around the engine and engine compartment. An effective way of doing this is to take a series of photographs of the various components before they are disconnected or removed. A simple inexpensive disposabie camera is ideal for this and the resulting photographs will prove invaluable when the engine is refitted.

Always be extremely careful when removing and refitting the engine/transmission. Serious injury can result from careless actions. Plan ahead and take your time, and a job of this nature, aithough major, can be accomplished successfully.

# Preparation for refitting

16The mating faces of the cylinder head and cylinder block must be perfectly clean before refitting the head. Citron recommend the use of a scouring agent for this purpose, but acceptable results can be achieved by using a hard plastic or wood scraper to remove all traces of gasket and carbon. The same method can be used to clean the piston crowns. Take particular care to avoid scoring or gouging the cylinder head/cylinder biock mating surfaces during the cleaning operations, as aluminium alloy is easily

damaged. Make sure that the carbon is not allowed to enter the oil and water passages - this is particularly important for the lubrication system, as carbon could block the oil supply to the engine's components. Using adhesive tape and paper, seal the water, oil and bolt hoies in the cylinder biock. To prevent carbon entering the gap between the pistons and bores, smear a little grease in the gap. After cleaning each piston, use a small brush to remove a traces of grease and carbon from the gap, then wipe away the remainder with a clean rag.

1Check the mating surfaces of the cylinder biock and the cylinder head for nicks, deep scratches and other damage. If slight, they may be removed carefuily with a file, but if excessive, machining may be the only aIternative to renewal. If warpage of the cylinder head gasket surface is suspected. use a straight-edge to check it for distortion. Refer to Section 9 if necessary.

18 Thoroughly clean the threads of the cylinder head bolt holes in the cylinder block. Ensure that the boits run freely in their threads, and that al traces of oil and water are removed from each bolt hole.

# Gasket selection

19 Tum the crankshaft until pistons 1 and 4 are at TDC. Position a dial test indicator (dial gauge) on the cylinder block, and zero it on the block face. Transfer the probe to the edge of No 1 piston, then slowly tum the crankshaft back and forth past TDC, noting the highest reading on the indicator. Record this reading. 20 Repeat this measurement procedure on No 4 piston, then turn the crankshaft half a tur (180°) and repeat the procedure on Nos 2 and 3 pistons (see Iustration).

21 f a dial test indicator is not available. piston protrusion may be measured using a straight-edge and feealer blades or vernier calipers. However, this is much less accurate. and cannot therefore be recommended.

22 Note down the greatest piston protrusion measurement, and use this to determine the correct cylinder head gasket from the fallowing table. The series of up to five notches on the side of the gasket are used for thickness identification (see illustration).

# Engine overhaul - dismanting sequence

11 Examine the head of each vaive for pitting, burming, cracks, and general wear. Check the valve stem for scoring and wear ridges. Rotate the valve, and check for any obvious indication that itis bent. Look for pits or excessive wear on the tip of each valve stem. Renew any valve that shows any such signs of wear or damage.

12If the valve appears satisfactory at this stage, measure the vaive stem diameter at several points using a micrometer (see illustration). Any significant difference in the readings obtained indicates wear of the valve stem. Should any of these conditions be apparent, the valve(sj must be renewed.

1f the valves are in satisfactory condition, they should be ground (apped) into their respective seats, to ensure a smooth, gastight seal. If the seat is only lightly pitted, or if it has been re-cut, fine grinding compound only should be used to produce the required finish. Coarse valve-grinding compound shouid nor be used, unless a seat is badly bumed or deeply pitted. If this is the case, the cylinder head and valves should be inspected by an expert, to decide whether seat recutting, or even the renewal of the valve or seat insert (where possible) is required.

14 Valve grinding is carried out as fallows. Place the head upside-down on blocks, on a bench.

15 Smear a trace of (the appropriate grade of vaive-grinding compound on the seat face. and press a suction grinding tool onto the valve head (see illustration). With a semirotary action, grind the valve head to its seat, ifting the valve occasionaly to redistribute the grinding compound. A light spring placed under the valve head will greatly ease this operation.

16 If coarse grinding compaund is being used, work only until a dul, matt even surface is produced on bath the valve seat and the alve, then wipe off the used compound, and repeat the process with fine compound, When a smooth unbroken ring of light grey matt finish is produced on both the valve and seat, the grinding operation is complete. Do not grind-in the valves any further than absolutely necessary, or the seat wil be prematurely sunk into the cylinder head.

Consult your Citroän dealer or engine specialist for further information on parts availability.

# 16 Main and big-end bearings - inspection

2 Bearing failure can occur due to lack of lubrication, the presence of dirt or other foreign particles, overoading the engine, or corrosion (see illustration). Regardless of the cause of bearing failure, the cause must be corrected (where applicable) before the engine is reassembled, to prevent it from happening again.

3 When examining the bearing shells, remove them from the cyinder block/crankcase, the main bearing ladder/caps (as appropriate), the connecting rods and the connecting rod bigend bearing caps. Lay them out on a clean surface in the same general position as their location in the engine. This will enable you to match any bearing problems with the corresponding crankshaft journal. Do not touch any shel's bearing surface with your fingers while checking it, or the delicate surface may be scratched.

4 Dirt and other foreign matter gets into the engine in a variety of ways. it may be left in the engine during assembly, or it may pass through fiters or the crankcase ventilation system. It may get into the oil, and from there into the bearings. Metal chips from machining operations and normal engine wear are often present. Abrasives are sometimes left in engine components after reconditianing. especially when parts are not tharoughly cleaned using the proper cleaning methods. Whatever the source, these foreign objects often end up embedded in the soft bearing material, and are easily recognised. Large particles will not embed in the bearing, and will score or gouge the bearing and journal. The best prevention for this cause of bearing falure is to clean all parts thoroughly. and keep everything spotiessly-clean during engine assembly, Frequent and regular engine oil and fiter changes are aiso recommended.

5 Lack of lubrication (or lubrication breakdown) has a number of interrelated causes. Excessive heat (which thins the oil). overloading (which squeezes the oil from the bearing face) and oil leakage (from excessive bearing clearances, worn ail pump or high engine speedsj all contribute to lubrication breakdown. Biocked oil passages, which usualy are the result of misaligned oi holes in a bearing shell, willaiso oil-starve a bearing. and destray it. When lack of lubrication is the cause of bearing failure, the bearing material is wiped or extruded from the steel backing of the bearing. Temperatures may increase to the point where the steel backing turns blue from overheating.

6 Driving habits can have a definite effect on bearing ife. Full-throttie, low-speed operation (labouring the engine) puts very high loads on bearings, tending to squeeze out the oil fim. These loads cause the bearings to flex, which produces fine cracks in the bearing face (fatigue failure). Eventually, the bearing material will loosen in pieces, and tear away from the steel backing.

Short-distance driving leads to corrosion of bearings, because insufticient engine heat is produced to drive off the condensed water and corrosive gases. These products coliect in the engine oil, forming acid and sludge. As the oil is carried to the engine bearings, the acid atacks and corrodes the bearing material.

8 Incorrect bearing installation during engine assembly will lead to bearing failure as wel. Tight-fitting bearings leave insufficient bearing running clearance, and will result in oll starvation. Dirt or foreign particles trapped behind a bearing shell result in high spots on the bearing, which lead to falure.

Do nof touch any shell's bearing surface with your fingers during reassembly; there is a risk of scratching the delicate surface, or of depositing particles of dirt on it.

10 As mentioned at the beginning of this Section, the bearing shelis should be renewed as a matter of course during engine overhaul: to do otherwise is false economy.

8 The clearance can be checked in either of two ways.

9 One method (which will be difficult to achieve without a range of internal micrometers or interal/external expanding calipers) is to refit the main bearing caps to the cylinder block/crankcase, with bearing shells in place. With the cap retaining bolts tightened to the specified torque, measure the internal diameter of each assembled pair of bearing shelis. If the diameter of each corresponding crankshaft joumal is measured and then subtracted from the bearing internal diameter, the result wil be the main bearing running clearance.

10The second (and more accurate) method is to use an American product known as Plastigauge. This consists of a fine thread of perfectly-round plastic, which is compressed between the bearing shell and the journal. When the shell is removed, the plastic is deformed, and can be measured with a special card gauge supplied with the kit. The running clearance is determined from this gauge. Piastigauge should be available from your Citroän dealer; otherwise, enquiries at one of the larger specialist motor factors shouid produce the name of a stockist in your area. The procedure for using Plastigauge is as follows.

14 Remove the main bearing caps, again taking great care not to disturb the Plastigauge or rotate the crankshaft.

15 Compare the width of the crushed Plastigauge on each joural to the scale printed on the Plastigauge envelope, to obtain the main bearing running clearance (see illustration). Compare the clearance measured with that in the Specifications at the start of this Chapter.

# General information and precautions

# General information

The cooling system is of pressurised type. comprising a coolant pump driven by the timing belt, an aluminium crossfiow radiator, expansian tank, electric cooling fan(s), a thermostat, heater matrix, and all associated hoses and switches.

The system functions as follows. Cold coolant in the bottom of the radiator passes through the bottom hose to the coolant pump. where it is pumped around the cylinder biock and head passages, and through the oill cooler(s (where fitted. After cooling the cylinder bores, combustion surfaces and valve seats. the cooiant reaches the underside of the thermostat, which is initialy closed. The coolant passes through the heater, and is retumed via the cylinder biock to the coolant pump.

When the engine is cold. the cooiant circulates only through the cylinder biock. cylinder head, and heater. When the coolant reaches a predetermined temperature, the thermostat opens, and the coolant passes through the top hose to the radiator. As the coolant circulates through the radiator, it is cooled by the in-rush of air when the car is in forward motion. The sirlow is supplemented by the action of the electric cooling fan(s when necessary. Upon reaching the bottam of the radiator, the coolant has now ccoled, and the cycle is repeated.

When the engine is at normal operating temperature, the coolant expands, and some of it is displaced into the expansion tank. Coolant coliects in the tank, and is returned to the radiator when the system cols.

On models with automatic transmission, a proportion of the coolant is recircutated from the bottom of the radiator through the transmission fluid cooler mounted on the transmission. On models fitted with an engine oil conler. the coolant is also passed through the of cooler.

The electric cooling fan(s) mounted adjacent to the radiator are controlled by a thermostatic switch/sensor. At a predetermined coolant temperature, the switch/sensor actuates the fan.

# Precautions

A Waring: Do not attempt to ea cooling system, while the engine is hot, as there is a high risk of scaiding. If the expansion tank filer cap must be removed before the engine and radiator have fuilly cooled (even though this is not recommended), the pressure in the cooling system must first be relieved. Cover the cap with a thick layer of cioth to avoid scalding, and slowly unscrew the filer cap until a hissing sound is heard. When the hissing has stopped, indicating that the pressure has reduced, siowly unscrew the filler cap until it can be removed; if more hissing sounds are heard, wait until they have stopped before unscrewing the cap. At all times, keep well away from the filer cap opening, and protect your hands.

A

Waming: Do not allow antifreeze to came into contact with your skin, or with the painted surfaces of the vehicle. Rinse off spills immediately, with plenty of water. Never ieave antifreeze lying around in an open container, or in a puddle in the driveway or on the garage floor. Children and pets are attracted by its sweet smell, but antifreeze can be fatal if ingested.

A

Waming: If the engine is hot, the electric cooling fan may start rotating even if the engine is not running. Be careful to keep your hands, hair, and any loose clothing well clear when working in the engine compartment.

A

Warming: Refer to Section 11 for precautions to be observed when working on models equipped with air conditioning.

# Heating and ventilation 0 system - general information

The heuting/ventilation system consists of a four-speed biower motor (housed behind the facia), face level vents in the centre and at each end of the facia, and air ducts to the front footwells.

The control unit is located in the facia, and the controlis operate flap vaives to deflect and mix the air flowing through the various parts of the heating/ventilation system, The flap valves are contained in the air distriution housing. which acts as a central distribution unit, passing air to the various ducts and vents.

Coid air enters the system through the grile at the rear of the engine compartment. If required, the airfow is boosted by the biower. and then fiows through the various ducts. according to the setings of the controls. Stale air is expelled through ducts at the rear of the vehicle. If warm air is required, the cold air is passed over the heater matrix, which is heated by the engine coolant.

On models fitted with air conditioning, a recirculation switch enables the outside air supply to be closed off, while the air inside the vehicle is recirculated. This can be useful to prevent unpieasant odours entering from outside the vehicle, but should only be used briefly, as the recirculated air inside the vehicle willsoon become stale.

11 Air conditioning system - general infomation and precautioions

# General information

An air conditioning system is available on certain models. It enables the temperature of incoming air to be lowered, and aiso dehumidities the air, which makes for rapid demisting and increased comfort.

The cooling side of the system works in the same way as a domestic refrigerator. Refrigerant gas is drawn into a belt-driven compressor, and passes into a condenser mounted on the front of the radiator, where it loses heat and becomes liquid. The liquid passes through an expansion valve to an evaporator, where it changes from liquid under high pressure to gas under low pressure. This change is accompanied by a drop in temperature, which cools the evaporator, The refrigerant returs to the compressor, and the cycle begins again.

Air blown through the evaporator passes to the air distribution unit, where it is mixed with hot air biown through the heater matrix to achieve the desired temperature in the passenger compartment.

The heating side of the system works in the same way as on models without air conditioning (see Section 9).

The operation of the system is controlied by an electronic control unit, which controls the electric cooling fan(s), the compressor and the facia-mounted warning light. Any problems with the system should be referred to a Citron dealer.

# Precautions

When an air conditioning system is fitted. is necessary to observe special precautions whenever dealing with any part of the system, or its associated components. if for any reason the system must be disconnected, entrust this task to your Citron deaier or a refrigeration engineer.

# A wstinc htai ogding refrigerant, and itis therefore dangerous to disconnect any part of the system without specialised knowledge and equipment.

The retrigerant is potentialy dangerous, and should only be handied by qualitied persons. i it is splashed onto the skin, it can cause frostbite. It is not itself poisonous, but ithe presence of a naked fame ncluding cigarette i forms a poisonous gas. Uncontrolled discharging of the refrigerant s dangerous, and potentially amaging to the environment.

# 1 General information and precautions

The fuel supply system consists of a fuel tank (which is mounted under the rear of the car, with an electric fuel pump immersed i i,. a fuel titer, fuel feed and retumn lines. The fuel pump supplies fuel to the fuel ral, which acts as a reservoir for the four fuel injectors which inject fuel into the inet tracts. The fuel fir incorporated in the feed line from the pump to the fuei rail ensures that the fuel supplied to the iniectors is clean.

Waring: Many of the procedures in this Chapter require the remaval of fuel lines and connections, which may result in some fuel spillage. Before carrying out any operation on the fuel system, refer to the precautions given in Safety first!' at the beginning of this manual, and follow them implicitly. Petrol is a highly dangerous and volatile liquid, and the precautions necessary when handlina it cannot be overstressed.

Refer to Section 6 for further information on the operation of each fuel injection system,

and to Section 17 for information on the exhaust system.

Note: Residual pressure will remein in the fuel ines long after the vehicie was last used. When disconnecting any fuel line, first depressurise the fuel systemn as descnbed in Section 7.

# Fuel injection systemsgeneral information

Note: The fuel injection ECU is of the 'seitlearning' type, meaning that as it operates, it afso monitors and stores the settings which give optimum engine performance under afl operating conditions. When the battery is disconnected, these settings are iost and the ECU reverts to the base settings programmed into its memory at the factory. On restarting. this may lead to the engine running/idling roughly for a short while, until the ECU has relearned the optimum settings. This process is best accomplished by taking the vehicie on a road test (for approximately 15 minutes). covering all engine speeds and loads, concentrating mainly in the 2500 to 3500 rpm region.

On all engines, the fuel injection and ignition functions are combined into a single engine management system, The systems titted are manufactured by Bosch, Sagem Lucas and Magneti Mareili, and are very similar to each other in most respects, the only significant differences being within the system ECUs. Each system incorporates a ciosed-loop catalytic converter and an evaporative emission contral system, and complies with the latest emission control standards. Refer to Chapter 5B tor information on the ignition side of each system; the fuel side of the system operates as follows.

The fuel pump supplies fuel from the tank to the fuel ral, via a replaceable cartridge fiter mounted underneath the rear of the vehicle. The pump itself is mounted inside the fuel tank, the pump motor is permanently immersed in fuel, to keep it cool. The fuel ra is mounted directly above the fuet injectors and acts as a fuel reservoir.

Fuel rail supply pressure is controlled by the pressure regulator, mounted at the end of the fuel rall or, on later Bosch systems, in front of the fuel tank. The regulator contains a spring loaded valve, which ifts to aliow excess fuel to return to the tank when the optimum operating pressure of the fuel system is exceeded (eg. during low speed, light load cruising. The regulator also contains a diaphragm which is supplied with vacuum from the iniet manifold. This allows the regulator to reduce the fuel supply pressure during light load, high manifold depression conditions (eg, during iding or deceleration) to prevent excess fuel being sucked' through the open injectors.

The fuel injectors are electromagnetic pintle vaives, which spray atomised fuel into the combustion chambers under the control of the engine managoment system ECU. There are four injectors, one per cylinder, mounted in the inlet manifoid close to the cylinder head. Each injector is mounted at an angle that aliows it to spray fuel directly onto the back of the inlet vaive(s). The ECU controis the volume of fuel injected by varying the length of tme for which each injector is held open.

The fuel injection systems are typically of the simultaneous injection type, whereby all four injectors open at the same time and fuel is injected into each cylinder's inlet tract twice per engine cycle; once during the power stroke and once during the induction stfoke. On later Bosch systems, however, sequential fuel injection is used whereby each injector coerates individually in cylinder sequence.

The electrical control systerm consists of the ECU, along with the following sensors:

a) Throttie potentiometer - informs the ECU of the throtte valve position, and the rate of throttie opening/closing.   
Coolant temperature sensor - informs the ECU of engine temperature.   
c Inlet air temperature sensor - informs the ECU of the temperature of the air passing through the throttle hausing.   
Lambda sensor - informs the ECU of he oxygen content of the exhaust gases (explained in greater detail in Part D of this Chapter).   
e Manifold pressure sensor - informs the ECU of the load on the engine (expressed in termns of inlet manifoid vacuum).   
Crankshaft sensor - informs the ECU of engine speed and crankshaft angular position.   
Vehicle speed sensor - informs the ECU of the vehicle speed.   
n Knock sensor - informs the ECU of preignition (detonation) within the cyinders. Not af systemns utilise this sensor.   
Camshaft sensor - informs the ECU of which cylinder is on the firing stroke on iater systems with sequential injection.

Signals from each of the sensors are compared by the ECU and, based on this information, the ECU selects the response appropriate to those values, and controls the fuel injectors (varying the pulse width - the length of time the injectors are held open - to provide a richer or weaker air/fuel mixture, as appropriate). The air/fuel mixture is constantly varied by the ECU, to provide the best settings for cranking, starting with either a hot or cold engine) and engine warm-up, idle. cruising and acceleration.

The ECU aiso has full control over the engine idie speed, typically via a stepper motor fitted to the throttie housing. The stepper motor pushrod controls the amount of air passing through a bypass driling at the side of the throttle. When the throttle vaive is closed (accelerator pedal released), the ECU uses the motor to alter the position of the pushrod, controlling the amount of air bypassing the throttle vaive and so controlling the idle spoed. The ECU aiso caries out fine tuning' of the idle speed by varying the ignition timing to increase or reduce the torque of the engine as it is idling. This helps to stabilise the idle speed when eiectrical or mechanical loads (such as headights, air conditioning, etc) are switched on and off.

On certain Bosch systems, ECU control of the engine idle speed is by means of an auxiliary air valve which bypasses the throttle valve. When the throttle valve is closed, the ECU controls the opening of the air valve. which in tum regulates the amount of air entering the manifold, and so controls the ide speed.

The throttle housing on most engines is fitted with an electric heating element. The heater is supplied with current by the ECU. warming the throttie hausing on coid starts to help prevent icing of the throtte vaive.

The exhaust and evaporative loss emission control systems are described in more detail in Chapter 4D.

If there is any abnormality in any of the readings obtained from the coolant temperature sensor, the inlet air temperature sensor or the lambda sensor, the ECU enters its "back-up' mode. If this happens, the erroneous sensor signal is overridden, and the ECU assumes a pre-programmed "back-up' value, which wil alow the engine to continue running, albeit at reduced efficiency. If the ECU enters this mode, the warning lamp on the instrument panel wil be illuminated. and the relevant fault code wil be stored in the ECU memory.

If the waming ight iluminates, the vehicle should be taken to a Citron dealer at the earliest opportunity. Once there, a complete test of the engine management system can be

carried out, using a special electronic diagnostic test unit, which is piugged into the system's diagnostic connector.

# General information

1 On 1.4 and 1.6 litre engines, the exhaust system consists of four sections: the frant pipe, the catalytic converter, the intermediate pipe and centre silencer, and the tallpipe and main silencer (see lustration). All exhaust sections are joined by a flanged joint. The front pipe jaints are secured by nuts and bolts, the catalytic converter joint being of the spring-loaded ba type, to alliow for movement in the exhaust system. The catalytic converter-to-intermediate pipe joint and the intermediate pipe-to-siencer joint are secured by a clamping ing.

2 On 1.8 and 2.0 litre engines, the exhaust system consists of three sections; the front pipe/catalytic converter, the intermediate pipe and centre silencer and the talpipe and main silencer. 3 The system is suspended throughout its entire length by rubber mountings.

# General information and precautions

# General information

The fuel system consists of a rear-mounted tuel tank, a fuel filter with integral water separator, a fuel injection pump, injectors and associated components. A turbocharger is fited to DHY (XUD9TE) and DHV (XUD9BSD) engines, together with an intercooler on the DHY unit

The exhaust system is conventional, but to meet the latest emission leveis an unregulated catalytic converter and an exhaust gas recirculation system are fitted to all modeis.

Fuel is drawn from the fuel tank to the fuel injection pump by a vane-type transfer pump incorporated in the fuel injection pump. Before reaching the pump, the fuel is heated by coolant flowing through the base of the thermostat/fuel fiter housing. The fuel then passes through a fuel fiter, where foreign matter and water are removed. Excess fuel lubricates the maving components of the pump, and is then neturmed to the tank.

The fuel injection pump is driven at halfcrankshaft speed by the timing belt. The high pressure required to inject the fuel into the compressed air in the swirt chambers is achieved by a cam piate acting on a single piston on the Bosch pump, or by two opposed pistons forced together by rolters running in a cam ring on the Lucas pump. The fuel passes through a central rotor with a single outiet driling which aligns with ports leading to the injector pipes.

Fuel meterning is controled by a centrifugal governor, which reacts to accelerator pedal position and engine speed. The governor is linked to a metering valve, which increases or decreases the amount of fuel delivered at each pumping stroke. On turbocharged modeis, a separate device also increases fuel delivery with increasing boost pressure.

Basic injection timing is determined when the pump is fitted. When the engine is running, it is varied automatically to suit the prevailing engine speed by a mechanism which tums the cam plate or ning.

The four fuel injectors produce a homogeneous spray of fuel into the swirt chambers located in the cylinder head. The injectors are calibrated to open and close at critical pressures to provide efficient and even combustion. Each injector needle is lubricated by fuel, which accumulates in the spring chamber and is channelled to the injection pump retum hose by leak-off pipes.

Bosch or Lucas fuel system components may be fitted, depending on engine type. Components from the latter manufacturer are marked either Lucas", 'CAV. "Roto-Diesel or Con-Diesel', depending on their date and place of manufacture. With the exception of the fuel fiter assembly, replacement components must be of the same make as those originally fitted.

Cold starting is assisted by preheater or glow plugs fitted to each swir chamber. Additionaly, a thermostatic sensor in the cooling system operates a fast ideever on the injection pump to increase the iding speed when the engine is cold.

A stop solenoid cuts the fuel supply to the injection pump rotor when the ignition is switched off, and there is also a handoperated stop lever for use in an emergency.

Provided that the specified maintenance is carried out, the fuel injection equipment wil give long and trouble-free service. The injection pump itseif may well outiast the engine. The main potential cause of damage to the injection pump and injectors is dirt or water in the fuel.

Servicing of the injection pump and injectors is very limited for the home mechanic, and any dismanting or adjustment other than that described in this Chaptar must be entrusted to a Citron dealer or fuel injection specialist.

# Diesel electronic control systems

Primarily to comply with incrsasingly stringent emission regulations, and to alliow an engine immobiliser facility to be incorporated into the venicle _anti-theft system, all Xsara diesel engines utilise electronic contral of certain functions. The extent of tha eiectronic control employed depends on the engine type and the teritory of export, wnich iargely governs the emission level of the particular engine.

The primary areas where electronic control is used are as follows. a Venicle anti-theft system. Exheust gas recirculation system. Preheating system.

On all engnes, the fuel injection pump stop solenoid is integral with an anti-theft module mounted on the side. or rear. of the injection pump. When the ignition key is removed from the lock, the stop solenoid is permanently deactivated by the anti-theft module, thus immobilising the engine. The engine wil remain immobilised until the anti-theft system recognises the insertion of a correctly-coded ignition key in the lock. Further information on the operation of the anti-theft system is contained in Chapter 12.

An exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) system is aiso fitted to all diesel engines. The EGR system reduces the level of nitrogen oxides produced during combustion by recirculating a proportion of the exhaust gases back into the iniet manifold under certain operating conditions. The operating conditions necessary for exhaust gas recirculation and the sensors supplying the necessary information are as follows.

a Engihe at normal operating temperature - coolant temperature switch/sensor signal.   
Engine operating under no load or part load conditions - throtte position switch/sensor signal.   
Engine speed above a specified value - crankshaft sensor signal (certain engines only.

Details of the EGR system operation are contained in Chapter 4D, Section 3.

The sensors listed above are also used for control of the preheating system, and supply information on engine temperature, and angine speed and load. Details of the preheating system operation are contained in Chapter 5C.

On DHV (XUD9BSD engine) models an electronic control unit (ECU) is used to control

the EGR system, the preheating system, and the injection timing of the fuel injection pump. The ECU uses the coolant temperature sensor signal. to determine engine temperature, and the crankshaft sensor signal to determine engine speed and position. In addition. information on tuel injector aperation is provided by a needle lift sansor incorporated into No 3 fuel injector, and information on throttle position and engine load is provided by a throttle position sensor fited to the injection pump control lever.

Further information on the vanious sensors will be found in Section 22.

2 All engines are fitted with a hand-operated priming pump, consisting of a rubber bulb, or pump plunger. On XUD series engines. the priming pump rubber bulb is located on the right-hand side of the engine compartment (see ilustration). On DW series engines, the priming pump plunger is located on the side of the fuel fiter assembly at the front of the engine. pressure circuit when it is primed. On engines without an automatic bleed valve, a bleed screw is fitted to the injection pump fuel inlet pipe union bolt (see illustration),. Where a bleed screw is tited, siacken the screw half a tur.

4 Pump the priming pump bulb or plunger until fuel free from air bubbies amerges from the bleed screw (where fited), or until resistance is felt. Retighten the bleed scpew.

6 if a large amount of air has entered the pump, place a wad of rag around the fuel returm union on the pump (to absort spilt tuel). then slacken the union. Tighten the union and mop up split fuel.

# XUD series engines

1 Checking the injection timing is not a routine operation, and should only be necessary after the injection pump has been disturbed.

2 The static timing procedure described in this Chapter must be carried out carefully to be accurate. A dial test indicator will be needed, with probes and adaptors appropriate to the type of injection pump. Read through the procedures bere sing work, to find out what is involved.

# DW series engines

3 Both types of fuel injection pump (Bosch and Lucas) are fited to the DW engine by means of non-adjustable mountings. This means that the static injection timing is fixed and cannot be adjusted by rotating the pump body with respect to the engne.The only way of checking that the timing is correct is to set the engine to TDC, as described in Chapter 2, Section 3. In this position, the tming hole in the ijection pump sprocket hub should line up with a corresponding hale in the injectin pump body, allowing the fitment of a sprocket locking toal. Misalignment of the timing holes means that the timing belt has been incorectly fitted.

# 10 Fuel injectors - testing. removal and refiting

Щ

Waming: Exercise extreme caution when working on the fuel injectors. Never expose the hands or any part of the body to injector spray, as the high working pressure can cause the fuel to penetrate the skin, with possibly fatai resuits. You are strongly advised to have any work which invoives testing the injectors under pressure carried out by a dealer or fuel injection speclalist.

# Testing

1Injectors do deteriorate with prolonged use, and it is reasonable to expect them to need reconditioning or renewal after 60 000 miles (100 000 km) oR so. AcCUraTe tESTING, overaUl and calibration of the injectors must be left to a specialist. A defective injector which is causing knocking or smoking can be located without dismanting as follows.

# 17 Turbocharger -

description and precautions

# Description

1 A turbocharger is fitted to some engines, It increases engine efficiency by raising the pressure in the iniet manifold above atmospheric pressure. Instead of the air simply being sucked into the cylinders, it is forced in. Additional fuel is supplied by the injection pump in proportion to the incressed air intake.

2 Energy for the operation of the turbocharger comes from the exhaust gas.

The gas flows through a specially-shaped housing the turbine housing and in so doing. spins the turbine wheel. The turbine whel is attached to a shaft, at the end of which is another vaned wheel known as the compressor wheei. The compressor wheel spins in its own housing, and compresses the et ir n the way to the iet manifold.

3 On DHY (XUDSTE engine) models, between the turbocharger and the inlet manifold, the compressed _air passes through an intercooler. This is an air-to-air heat exchanger, mounted over the engine, _and supplied with cooling air ducted through the bonnet insulation. The purpose of the intercooler is to remove some of the heat gained in being compressed from the inlet ar. Because cooler air is denser, removal of this heat further increases engine efficiency.

4 Boost pressure (the pressure in the iniet manifold is limited by a wastegate, which diverts the exhaust gas away from the turbine wheel in response to a pressure-sensitive actuator.

5 The turbo shaft is pressure-lubricated by an oll feed pipe from the main oil gallery. The shat "iats' on a cushion of ol A drain pipe retumns the oi to the sump.

# Precautions

6The turbocharger operates at extremely high speeds and temperatures. Certain precautions must be observed to avaid premature falure of the turbo, or injury to the aperator.

# General information

1 All diesel engines covered in this Chapter utise slectronic control of certain functions. The number and type of sensors, actuators and associated components used on a particular engine depends on the engine type. territory of export and emission level. The tollowing information is therefore provided as a general guide to the components that may be encountered, according to engine type.

# Electronic Control Unit (ECU)

2 An ECU is used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis to contral the injection timing. preheater glow plug operation and the exhaust gas recirculation system. The ECU receives signals from sensors, which monitor engine coolant temperature, engine speed. fuel injector operation and engine load. These signals are used by the ECU to control the previously mentioned system functions.

# Crankshaft sensor

3 This is an inductive pulse generator balited to the transmission bellhousing, to scan a reference ridge on the flywheeil. As the ridge passes the sensor tip, a signal is generated, which is used by the ECU, or the EGR system, to determine engine speed. The crankshaft sensor is used on ai engines.

# Coolant temperature sensor/switch

4 The coolant temperature sensor is an NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) thermistar - that is, a semi-conductor whose electrical resistance decreases as its temperature increases. The sensor supplies a constantlyarying(analogue)voltage signal. corresponding to the temperature of the engine coolant. The sensor is used for control of the EGR system and preheating system and, on HV (XUD9BSD engine) models, is aiso used to refine the calculations made by the ECU when determining fuel metering. On some modets, the sensar consists simply of a switch whose internal contacts close once a predetermined coolant temperature has been attained.

# Throttle position switch

5 The throttle position switch is fitted to all except DHV (XUD9BSD engine) models, and s located on the top of the injection pump.

attached to the pump control lever. The switch contacts close when the pump control lever has moved through a set distance, thus providing an engine load signal for the EGR and preheating systems.

# Throttle position sensor

6 The throttle position sensor is used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis, and is located on the top of the injection pump, attached to the pump control lever. The unit consists of a potentiometer whose resistance varies according to accelerator position. From this information, the ECU can regulate the fuel injection timing according to driver input and engine load.

# Injector needle lift sensor

7 The needie lift sensor, used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) models, is an integral part of No 3 fuel injector, and sends a signal to the ECU whenever the injector opens.

# Preheating system control unit

This unit is fitted to all models and operates the preheating system giow plugs during cold staring conditions. On DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis, the unit is controlled by the ECU.

9 Introduction of part of the exhaust gas back into the iniet manifold is controlled by an EGR solenoid valve and EGR vacuum valve. Vacuum trom the engine vacum pump is directed to the EGR solenoid valve. When the solenoid valve is actuated (depending on coolant temperature and angine load or speed) the vacuum is diverted to the vacuum valve, thus opening the valve.
