# General information

The bodyshel is made of pressed-steel sections, and is available in three-door Coupe, five-door Hatchback, and five-door Estate versions. Most components are weided together, but some use is made of structural adhesives. The front wings are bolted on.

The bonnet, doors and some other vuinerable paneis are made of zinc-coated metal, and are further protected by being coated with an anti-chip primer prior to being sprayed.

Extensive use is made of plastic materiais, mainly in the interior, but also in exterior components. The front and rear bumpers and the front grile are injection-mouided from a synthetic material which is very strong. yet light. Plastic components such as wheelarch liners are fitted to the underside of the vehicle. to improve the body's resistance to corosion.

# 2 Maintenancebodywork and underframe

The general condition of a vehicie's bodywork is the one thing that significantly affects its value. Maintenance is easy, but needs to be regular. Neglect. particuiarly after minor damage, can lead quickly to further deterioration and costly repair bilis. It is important also to keep watch on those parts of the vehicle not immediately visible, for instance the underside, inside all the wheelarches, and the lower part of the engine compartment.

The basic maintenance routine for the bodywork is washing - preferably with a lot of water, from a hose. This will remove all the loose solids which may have stuck to the vehicle. It is important to flush these off in such a way as to prevent gnit from scratching the finish. The wheelarches and underframe need washing in the same way, to remove any accumulated mud which will retain moisture and tend to encourage rust. Paradoxically enough, the best time to ciean the undertrame and wheelarches is in wet weather, when the mud is thoroughly wet and soft. In very wet weather, the underframe is usualy cleaned of large accumulations automatically, and this is a good time for inspection.

Periodicaly, except on vehicies with a waxbased underbady protective coating.  is a good idea to have the whole of the underrame of the vehicie steam-cleaned, engine compartment included, so that a thorough inspection can be carried out to see what minor repairs and renovations are necessary. Steam-cleaning is available at many garages, and is necessary for the removal of the accumulation of oily grime, which sometimes is alowed to becorne thick in certain areas. If steam-cieaning facilities are not available. there are one or two excellent grease solvents avaiable, which can be brush-appied: the dirt can then be simply hosed off. Note that these methods should not be used on vehicles with wax-based underbody protective coating, or the coating will be remaved. Such vehicles should be inspected annually, preferably just prior to winter, when the underbody should be washed down, and any damage to the wax coating repared using underseal. Ideally, a completely fresh coat should be applied. It would also be worth considering the use of wax-based protection for injection into door paneis, sils, box sections, etc, as an additional safeguard against rust damage. where such protection is not provided by the vehicle manufacturer.

After washing paintwork, wipe off with a chamois leather to give an unspotted clear finish. A coat of clear protective wax polish will give added protection against chemical pollutants in the air. Iif the paintwork sheen has dulled or oxidised, use a cleaner/polisher combination to restore the briliance of the shine. This requires a little effort, but such dulling is usually caused because regular washing has been neglected. Care needs to be taken with metalic paintwork, as a special non-abrasive cleaner/polisher is required to avoid damage to the finish, Always check that the door and ventilator opening drain holes and pipes are completely clear, so that water can be drained out. Brightwork should be treated in the same way as paintwork. Windscreens and windows can be kept clear of the smeary fim which often appears, by the use of proprietary glass cleaner. Never use any form of wax or other body or chromium polish on glass.

# 3 Maintenanceupholstery and carpets

Mats and carpets should be brushed or vacuum-cieaned regularly, to keep them free of grit. if they are badly stained, remove them from the vehicie for scrubbing or sponging. and make quite sure they are dry before refitting, Seats and interior trim paneis can be kept clean by wiping with a damp cloth and a proprietary upholstery cleaner. If they do become stained (which can be more apparent on light-coloured upholstery), use a littleliquid detergent and a soft nail brush to scour the grime out of the grain of the material. Do not forget to keep the headlining clean in the same way as the uphoistery. When using liquid cleaners inside the vehicle, do not overwet the surfaces being cleaned. Excessive damp could get into the seams and padded interior, causing stains, offensive odours or even rot. If the inside of the vehicle gets wet accidentally, it is worthwhile taking some trouble to dry it out properly, particularly where carpets are involved.

Caution: Do not leave oll or electric heaters inside the vehicie for this purpose.

Minor body damage - repair

вЩ

# Repairs of minor scratches in bodyworkork

It the scratch is very superficial, and does not penetrate to the metal of the bodywork. repair is very simple. Lightly rub the area of the scratch with a paintwork renovator, or a very fine cuting paste, to remove laose paint trom the scratch, and to ciear the surrounding bodywork of wax polish. Rinse the area with clean water.

Apply touch-up paint to the scratch using a fine paint brust; continue to apply fine layers of paint unti the surface of the paint in the scratch is level with the surrounding paintwork. Allow the new paint at least two weeks to harden, then blend it into the surrounding paintwork by rubbing the scratch area with a paintwork renovator or a very fine cutting paste. Finally apply wax polish.

Where the scratch has penetrated right through to the metal of the bodywork, causing the metal to rust, a different repar technique is required. Remove any loose rust from the bottom of the scratch with a penknife, then apply rust-inhibiting paint, to prevent the formation of rust in the future. Using a rubber or nylon applicator, fil the scratch with bodystopper paste. If required, this paste can be mixed with cellulose thinners, to provide a very thin paste which is ideal for filing narrow scratches. Before the stopper-paste in the scratch hardens, wrap a piece of smooth cotton rag around the top of a finger. Dip the finger in cellulose thinners, and quickly sweep it across the surface of the stopper-paste in the scratch; this will ensure that the surface of the stopper-paste is slightly hollowed. The scratch can now be painted over as described earlier in this Section.

# Repairs of dents in bodywork

When deep denting of the vehicle's bodywork has taken place, the first task is to pull the dent out, unti the affected bodywork aimost attains its original shape. There is litle point in trying to restore the original shape completely, as the metal in the damaged area wil have stretched on impact, and cannot be reshaped fully to its original contour. It is better to bring the level af the dent up to a point which is about 3 mm below the level of the surrounding bodywork. In cases where the dent is very shalliow anyway, it is not worth tying to pul it out at al if the underside of the dent is accessible, it can be hammered out gently from behind, using a mallet with a wooden or plastic head. Whilst doing this. hoid a suitable block of wood firmly against the outside of the panei, to absorb the impact from the hammer blows and thus prevent a large area of the bodywork from being "belledour'.

Should the dent be in a section of the bodywork which has a double skin, or some other factor making it inaccessible trom behind, a different technique is called for, Drill several small holes through the metal inside the area - particularly in the deeper section. Then screw long selt-tapping screws into the holes, just sufficiently for them to gain a good purchase in the metal. Now the dent can be pulled out by puling on the protruding heads of the screws with a pair of pliers.

The next stage of the repair is the removal of the paint from the damaged area, and from an inch or so of the surrounding 'sound' bodywork. This is accomplished most easily by using a wire brush or abrasive pad on s power drill, aithough it can be done just as effectively by hand, using sheets of abrasive paper. To complete the preparation for filing, score the surface of the bare metal with a screwdriver or the tang of a file, or alternatively, drill small holes in the affected area. This will provide a really good 'key' for the filter paste.

To complete the repair, see the Section on iling and respraying.

# Repairs of rust holes or gashes in bodyworrk

Remove all paint from the affected area, and from an inch or so of the surrounding 'sound' bodywork, using an abrasive pad or a wire brush on a power dil. If these are not available, a few sheets of abrasive paper will do the job most effectively. With the paint removed, you will be abie to judge the severity of the corrosion, and therefore decide whether to renew the whole panel (if this is possibie) or to repair the affected area. New body panels are not as expensive as most people think, and it is often quicker and more satisfactory to fit a new panel than to attempt to repair large areas of corosion.

Remove al fttigs from the affected area, except those which will act as a guide to the original shape of the damaged bodywork (eg headlight shelis etc),. Then, using tin snips or a hacksaw blade, remove alloose metal and any other metal badly affected by corrosion. Hammer the edges of the hole inwards, in order to create a slight depression for the flier paste.

Wire-brush the affected area to remove the powdery rust from the surface of the remaining metal. Paint the affected area with rust-inhibiting paint; if the back of the rusted area is accessible, treat this also.

Before filing can take place, it will be necessary to block the hole in some way. This can be achieved by the use of aluminium or plastic mesh, or aluminium tape.

Aluminium or plastic mesh, or glass-fibre mattig. is probably the best material to use for a large hole. Cut a piece to the approximate size and shape of the hole to be filed, then position it in the hole so that its edges are below the level of the surrounding bodywork. It can be retained in pasition by several blobs of filer peste around s periphery

Aluminium tape should be used for smalil or very narrow holes. Pull a piece off the roll, trim it to the approximate size and shape required. then puli of the backing paper if used and stick the tape over the hole: it can be overliapped if the thickness of one piece is insufficient. Burnish down the edges of the tape with the handle of a screwdriver or similar, to ensure that the tape is securely attached to the metal underneath.

# Bodywork repairs – filing and respraying

Before using this Section, see the Sections on dent, minor scratch, rust holes and gash repairs.

Many types of bodyfiller are available, but generally speaking. those proprietary kits which contain a tin of filler paste and a tube of resin hardener are best for this type of repair; some can be used directly from the tube. A wide, fexibie plastic or nylon applicator will be found invaluable for imparting a smooth and welcontoured finish to the surce of the fller.

Mix up a little filer on a clean piece of card or board - measure the hardener carefully (follow the maker's instructions on the pack). othenwise the filer will set too rapidly or too slowly. Using the applicator, apply the filer paste to the prepared area; draw the applicator across the surface of the filer to achieve the correct contour and to level the surface. As soon as a contour that approximates to the correct one is achieved, stop working the paste - if you carry on too long. the paste will became sticky and begin to pick-up' on the applicator. Continue to add thin layers of filler paste at 20-minute intervals, until the level of the filer is just proud of the surrounding bodywork.

Once the flier has hardened, the excess can be removed using a metal plane or fie. From then on, pragressively-finer grades of abrasive paper should be used, starting with a 40-grade production paper, and finishing with a 400-grade wet-and-dry paper. Always wrap the atrasive paper around a flat rubber, oork. or wooden block - otherwise the surface of the fller wil not be compietely fliat. During the smoothing of the file surtace, the wet-anddry paper should be periodically rinsed in water. This will ensure that a very smooth fiish is med to the filer at the ial stage.

At this stage, the 'dent' should be surrounded by a ring of bare metal, which in tum should be encircled by the finely feathered' edge of the good paintwork. Rinse the repair area with clean water, until all of the dust produced by the rubbing-down operation has gone.

Spray the whoie area with a light coat of primer - this wil show up any imperfections in the surface of the filer. Repair these imperfections with fresh filer paste or bodystopper, and once _more smooth the surface with abrasive paper. If bodystopper is used, it can be mixed with cellulose thinners. to form a really thin paste which is ideal for tiling small holes. Repeat this spray-andrepair procedure until you are satisfied that the surface of the fier, and the feathered edge of the paintwork, are perfect. Clean the repair aewith can water, andllw to dy fuly.

The repair area is now ready for final spraying. Paint spraying must be carried out in a warm, dry, windiess and dust-free atmosphere. This condition can be created artificially if you have access to a large indoor working area, but if you are forced to work in the open, you wil have to pick your day very carefuly. If you are working indoors, dousing the floor in the work area with water will help to settle the dust which would otherwise be in the atmosphere. If the repair area is confined to one body panel, mask aoft the surrounding panels: this will help to minimise the effects of a slight mismatch in paint colours. Bodywork fittings (eg chrome strips, door handies etc) will iso need to be masked off. Use genuine masking tape, and several thicknesses of newspaper, for the masking operations.

Before commencing to spray, agitate the aerosol can thoroughly, then spray a test area (an old tin, or similar) until the technique is mastered, Cover the repair area with a thick coat of primer; the thickness should be bult up using several thin layers of paint, rather than one thick one. Using 400 grade wet-anddry paper, rub down the surface of the primer unti it is really smooth. While doing this, the work area should be thoroughly doused with water, and the wet-and-dry paper periodicaly nised in water. Alow to dry before spraying on more paint.

Spray on the top coat, again building up the thickness by using several thin layers of paint. Start spraying at the top of the repair area. and then, using a side-to-side motion, work downwards until the whole repair area and about 2 inches of the surrounding original paintwork is covered. Remove all masking material 10 to 15 minutes after spraylng on the finai coat of paint.

Aliow the new paint at least two weeks to harden, then, using a paintwork renovator or a very fine cutting paste, blend the edges of the paint into the existing paintwork. Finally, apply wax polish.

# Plastic components

Witn the use of more and more plastic body component y the ehicemanfacturersg bumpers. spoilers, and in some cases major body paneis), rectification of more serious damage to such items has become a matter of either entrusting repair work to a specialist in this field or renewing complete components. Repair of such damage by the

DIY owner is not realy feasible, owing to the cost of the equipment and materiais required for effecting such repairs. The basic technique involves making a groove along the line of the crack in the plastic, using a rotary burr i a power drill The damaged part is then welded back togather, using a hot ar gun to heat up and fuse a plastic filer rod into the groove. Any excess plastic is then removed, and the area rubbed down to a smooth finish. It is important that a filler rod of the correct plastic is used, as body components can be made of variety of different types (og polycarbonate. ABS, polypropylene).

Damage of s less serious nature (abrasions, minor cracks etc can be repaired by the DY owner using a two-part epoxy filer repair material. Once mixed in equal propartions. this is used in simiar fashion to the bodywork fie uedon malpaeshe fileris usualy cured in twenty to thirty minutes, ready for sanding and painting.

If the owner is renewing a complete component himself, or if he has repaired it with epoxy filer, he wil be left with the problem of finding a suitable paint for finishing which is compatible with the type of plastic used. At one time, the use of a universal paint was not possibie, owing to the complex range of plastics encountered in body camponent applications Standard paints, generally speaking, will not bond to plastic or rubber satisfactorily. However, it is now posaible to obtain a plastic body parts finishing kit which consists of a pre-primer treatment, a primer and coloured top coat. Ful instructions are normally supplied with a kit, but basically, the method of use is to first apply the pre-primer to the component concered, and aliow it to dry for up to 30 minutes. Then the primer is applied, and left to dry for about an hour before finally applying the special-coloured top coat. The result is a correctly-coloured component, where the paint will flex with the plastic or rubber, a property that standard paint does not normally posses.

# 5Major body damage - repair

Where serious damage has occurred, or large areas need renewal due to neglect, it means that compiete new panels will need weiding-in, and this is best left to professionals. If the damage is due to impact, it wil also be necessary to check completely the alignment of the bodyshel, and this can only be carried out accurately by a Citroen deasier, or accident repair specialist, using special jigs. If the body is left misaligned, it is primarily dangerous, as the car will not handie properly, and secondly, uneven strasses will be imposed on the steering, suspension and possibly transmission, causing abnormal wear, or complete failure, particularly to such items as the tyres.

# General information and precautions

# Waring: Before carrying out any work on the electrical system, read through the precautions given in 'Safety first at the beginning of this manual, and in Chapter 5A.

The electrical system is of 12-volt negative earth type. Power for the lights and all electrical accessories is supplied by a leadacid type battery, which is charged by the atternator.

This Chapter covers repair and service procedures for the various electrical components not associated with the engine. Information on the battery, alternator and starter motor can be found in Chapter 5A.

I should be noted that, prior to working on any component in the electrical system, the battery negative terminal should first be disconnected, to prevent the possibility of electrical short-circuits.

Caution: Before proceeding, refer to Disconnecting the battery in the Reference Section of this manual for further information.

# Electrical fault indinggeneral information

Note: Refer to the precautions given in "Safety first' and in Section 1 of this Chapter before starting work. The foilowing fests relate to testing of the main electrical circuits, and should not be used to test delicate electronic circuits (such as engine management systems or anti-lock braking systems), particularly where an electronic control unit is used.

# General

1 A typical electrical circult consists of an electrical component, any switches, relays. motors, fuses, fusible links or circuit breakers related to that component, and the wiring and connectors which ink the component to both the battery and the chassis. To heip to pinpoint a probiem in an electrical circuit. wiring diagrams are included at the end of this Chapter.

2 Before attempting to diagnose an electrical fault, first study the appropriate wiring diagram, to obtain a more compiete understanding of the components included in the particular circult concemed. The possible sources of a fault can be narrowed down by noting whether other components related to the circuit are operating properly. If several components or circuits fail at one time, the problem is likely to be related to a shared fuse or earth connection.

3 Electrical problems usually stem from simple causes, such as loose or corroded connections, a faulty earth connection, a blown fuse, a melted fusible link, or a faulty relay. Visually inspect the condition of all fuses, wires and connections in a problem circuit before testing the components. Use the wiring diagrams to determine which terminal connections will need to be checked, in order to pinpoint the trouble-spot.

4 The basic toois required for electrical fault finding include a circult tester or voltmeter (a 12-valt bulb with a set o test leadS can also be used for certain tests); a seif-powered test light (sometimes known as a continuity tester): an ohmmeter (to measure resistancej; a battery and set of test leads: and a jumper wire, preferably with a circuit breaker or fuse incorporated, which can be used to bypass suspect wires or electrical components. Before attempting to locate a problem with test instruments, use the wiring diagram to determine where to make the connections.

5 To find the source of an intermitent wiring fault (usually due to a poor or dirty connection, or damaged wiring insulation), a wiggle' test can be performed on the wiring. This involves wiggling the wining by hand, to see if the fault occurs as the wining is moved. It should be possible to narrow down the source of the fault to a particular saction of wiring. This method of testing can be used in conjunction with any of the tests described in the folowing sub-Sections.

6 Apart from problems due to poor connections, two basic types of fauit can occur in an electrical circuit - apen-circuit, or shor-circult.

7 Open-circuit taults are caused by a break somewhere in the circuit, which prevents current from flowing. An open-circult fault will prevent a companent from working, but will not cause the relevant circuit fuse to blow.

Short-circuit faults are normally caused by a breakdown in wiring insulation, which allows a feed wire to touch either anothe wire, or n earthed component such as the bodyshell. This allows the current flowing in the ciruit to 'escape' along an alternative route, usually to earth. As the circuit does not now follow its original compiete path, it is known as a 'short' circult. A short-circult tault wil normaly cause the relevant circuit fuse to biow.

# Finding an open-circuit

9 To check for an open-circuit, connect one lead of a circuit tester or voitmeter to either the negative battery terminal or a known good earth.

1Connect the other lead to a connector in the circuit being tested, preferably nearest to the battery or fuse.

Switch on the circuit, baring in mind that some circuits are live only when the ignition switch is moved to a particular position.

1If voltage is present indicated either by the tester bul lighting or a volmeter reading. as applicable), this means that the section of the circuit between the relevant connector and the battery is problem-free.

13 Cantinue to check the remainder of the circuit in the same fashion.

14 When a point is reached at which no voltage is present, the problerm must lie between that point and the previous test point with voltage. Most problems can be traced to a broken, corroded or loose connection.

# Finding a short-circuit

15 To check tor a short-circuit, first disconnect the load(s) from the ciroult foads are the components which draw current from a circuit, such as bulbs, motors, heating elements, etc.

Remove the relevant fuse from the circut, and connect a circuit tester or voltmeter to the fuse connections.

17Switch on the circuit, beaning in mind that some circuits are live only when the ignition switch is moved to a particular position.

18 If voltage is present (indicated either by hetester bulighing or a voeteading. as applicable). this means that there is a short-circult.

19If no voltage is present, but the fuse stil blows with the load(s) connected, this indicates an intemal fault in the loadis).

# Finding an earth fault

20 The battery negative terminal 1s connected to 'earth' - the metal of the engine/transmission and the car body - and most systems are wired so that they only receive a positive feed, the current returming via the metal of the car body. This means that the component mounting and the body form part of that circuit. Loose or corroded mountings can therefore cause a range of electrical faults, ranging from total failure of a circuit, to a puzzing partial fault. In particular, lights may shine dimly (especially when another circuit sharing the same earth point is in operation), motors (eg wiper motors or the radiator cooling fan mator) may run slowly. and the operation of one circuit may have an apparently-unrelated effect on another. Note that earth straps are used between certain components, such as the engine/transmission and the body, usually where there is no metal to-metal contact between components, due to flexible rubber mountings, etc.

21 To check whether a component is property earthed, disconnect the battery, and connect one lead of an ohmmeter to a known good earth point. Cannect the other lead to the wire or earth connection being tested. The resistance reading should be zero; if not, check the connection as follows.

22 if an earth connection is thought to be fauity, dismantle the connection, and clean back to bare metal both the bodyshall and the wire terminal or the component earth connection mating surface. Be careful to remove al traces of dirt and corrosion, then use a knife to trim away any paint, so that a clean metal-to-metal joint is made. On reassembly. tighten the joint fasteners securely; if a wire terminal is being refitted.

# 3.3a For access to the fuses, remove the cover from the interiar fuse/relay box ...

use serrated washers between the terminal and the bodyshel, to ensure a clean and secure connection. When the connection is remade, prevent the onset of corosion in the future by applying a coat of petroleum jelly or silicone-based grease, or by spraying on (at regular intervals a proprietary inition seaer or water-dispersant lubricant.

# 3Fuses and relays - general information

# Fuses

1 Fusas are designed to break a circuit when a predetermined current is reached, in order to protect the components and wiring which could be damaged by excessive curent flow. Any excessive curent flow will be due to a fauit n the cirouit, usualy a short-circut (see Section 2.

2 The main fuses are located in the interior fuse/reliay box below the steering column on e drivr's sideof he aciand in te ee compartment fuse/relay box on the left-hand side of the engie compartment.

3 For access to the interior fuses, pul the fuse/relay box cover from the facia. For access to the engine compartment fuses, it off the cover over the fuse/relay box (see llustrationos).

4 A blown fuse can be recognised from its meited ar broken wire. 5 To remove a fuse, first ensure that the relevant circuit is switohed off.

6 Using the plastic toal provided in the fuseela boxpul the uefrom i location (see itustration).

7 Spare fuses are provided in the blank terminal positions in the fuse/relay box.

Betore renewing a blown fuse, trace and rectify the cause, and always use a fuse of the correct rating. Never substitute a fuse o a higher rating or make temporary repairs using wire or metal foil; more sericus damage, or even fire, could resuilt.

10Additional max-fuses' are located in the engine compartment fuse/relay box. These are generally known as fusible links' and carry a heavy current for the major vehicle circuits. Fusible links do not normally biow, but if they do, this indicates a major circuit falure or short-circut.

11 A relay is an electricaly-operated switch which is used for the following reasons: a A relay can switch a heavy cument emoly fo th ciut nwh te current is flowing, allowing the use

of ighter gauge wiring and switch cantacts. A relay can receive more than one contr input, unike a mechanical switch. A relay can have a timer function - for example, the intermittent wicer ralav.

13If a crcult or system controlled by a rel develops a fauilt, and the relay is suspec eh i should be possible to hear it 'click' as it energised.  this is the case, the fault lies wit the components or wiring of the system. relay is not being energised, then eithe the relay is not receiving a main supply or switching voltage or the relay itseif is fault Testing is by the substitution of a known goo unit, but be careful - while some relays ar identical in appearance and in operation, other look simliar but perform different functions.

14To remove a relay, first ensure that th relevant circuit is switched off In most caset the reiay can then simply be pulled out fror the socket, and pushed back into position Note, however, that with the ever increasing standardisation of vehicle wiring and electrica system components, many relays are nor welded' in position in their relevant circui boards for ease of manufacture. This meane that the relays are soldered in place anc cannot be individually removed. If faulty. the complete circuit board or relay housing mus be renewed as an assembly. Changes of thit nature ocour regularly during the course o vehicle production and are not normally documented by the vehicle manufacturer. Therefore, i a relay appears reluctant to come free from its lacation, consider that it may be of the welded type and consult a Citroér deaier for the latest information.

1Accurate adjustment of the headight beam is only possible using optical beam-setting equipment, and this work should therefore be carried out by a Citron dealer or suitablyequipped workshop.

2 Each headlight unit is equipped with a fiveposition vertical beam adjuster unit - this can be used to adjust the headlight beam to compensate for the relevant load which the

vehicle is carrying. The adjuster units are operated by a switch on the facia. The adjusters should be positioned as follows according to the load being carried in the vehicie:

Pasition 0 Front seats occupied (1 or 2 peaple)   
PositionFront or rear seats occupied (3 people)   
Position 1 Front and rear seats occupied (5 people)   
Position 2 Front and rear seats occupled and luggage compartment fully-loaded   
Position 3 Driver's seat occupied and uggage compartment fuly lodded

3 Be sure to reset the adjustment if the vehicle load is altered.

20 Anti-theft alarm system and engine immobiliser general information

\*

Note: This information is applicable only to the anti-theft alarm system fited by Citron as standard equipment.

# General

All models in the range are fitted with an anti-theft aiarm system as standard or optional equipment. The alarm is automaticaly armed and disarmed using the remote central locking transmitter (where applicable), When the system is activated, the alarm indicator light, located on the facia, wll flash continuously. In addition to the alarm function, the system also incorporates an angine immobiliser activated by a transponder in the ignition key.

# Anti-theft alarm system

Note that if the doors are operated using the key, the alarm will not be armed or disarmed (as applicabie),. If for some reason the remote central locking transmitter fails whilst the alarm is armed, the alarm can be disarmed using the key. To do this, open the door with the key, then anter the vehicle. noting that the alarm will sound as the door is opened. Switch on the ignitian, and once the ignition key is recognised, the alarm wil be disarmed.

The alarm system has switches on the bonnet, taiigate and each of the doors. It also has ultrasonic sensing, which detects movement inside the vehicle, via sensors mounted on either side of the vehicie interior. f required, the ulrasonic sensing facity can be switched of, whilst retaining the switched side of the system. To switch off the ultrasonic sensing. with the ignition switched off, depress the alarm switch located on the facia unti the alarm indicator light on the facia is continuously Iit. Now, when the doors are locked using the remote central locking transmitter, and the alarm is armed, only the switched side of the alarm system is operational (and the alarm indicator light will revert to its fiashing mode. This facility is useful, as it aliows you to leave the windows/sunroof open, and stil arm the alarm. It the windows/sunroof are ieft open with the ultrasonic sensing not switched off, the alarn may be faisely triggered by a gust of wind.

Should the alarm system become faulty, the vehicle should be taken to a Citron dealer for examination.

# Engine immobiliser

An electronic engine immobiliser is incorporated as part of the anti-theft system. The electronic immobiliser consists of a transponder fitted to the ignition key, and an analogue module fitted around the ignition switch. The system is controlled by the passenger compartment body computer.

When the ignition key is inserted in the switch and tumed to the ignition on position, the contral module sends a pre-programmed recognition code signal to the anaiogue madule on the ignition switch. if the recognition code signal matches that of the transponder on the ignition key, an uniocking request signal is sent to the engine management ECU, or injection pump antitheft module allowing the engine to be started. If the ignition key signal is not recognised, the engine management system remains immobilised.

When the ignition is switched off, a locking signal is sent to the ECU, or pump anti-theft module and the engine is immobiised until the unlocking request signal is again received.

The recognition code is programmed into the system during manufacture and is contained on a confidential card supplied with the veticle. The card should be kept in s safe place - never in the vehicle. The confidential card will be required if any work is to be camied out on the system by a Citron dealer, or if eplacement keys are required.

# Disconnecting the vehicle batery

Refer to Disconnecting the battery in the Reference Section of this manual).

21 Air bag system - general ifomation, precautions and system de-activation

# General information

A driver's air bag is fitted as standard equipment on certain models, and is an option an all other models. The air bag is fitted in the steering wheel centre pad. Additionally. a passenger's air bag located in the facia, and side air bags located in the front seats are also availabie.

The system is armed only when the ignition is switched on, however, a reserve power source maintains a power supply to the system in the event of a break in the main electrical supply, The steering wheel and facia air bags are activated by a 'g' sensor (deceleration sensor), and controlled by an electronic contral unit located under the centre console. The side air bags are activated by severe side impact and operate independently of the main system and of each other. A separate electrical supply and control unit is provided for each side air bag.

The air bags are inflated by a gas generator., which forces the bag out from its location in the steering wheel, facia or seat back frame.

# Precautions

A

Waming: The following precautions must be observed when working on vehicies equipped with an air bag

system, to prevent the possiblity of personal injury.

# General precautions

The tollowing precautions must be observed when carrying out work on a vehicle equipped with an air bag:

a Do not discannect the battery with the engine running.   
Before carrying out any work in the vicinity of the ar bag, removal of any of the air bag components, or any welding work on the vehicie, de-activate the system as descnibed in the following sub-Section.   
Do not attempt to test any of the air bag system circuits using test meters or any other test equipment.   
f the air bag waring ight comes on, ar any fault in the system is suspected, consult a Citron dealer without delay. Do not attempt to carry out fault diagnosis, or any dismanting of the components.

# Precautions to be taken when handing an ar ba

aTransport the air bag by itsef, bag upward   
o not put your arms around the air bag.   
Cary the ar bag close to the body, bag outward.   
Do not drop the air bag or expose it to impacts.   
Do not attempt to dismantle the air beg unit.   
Do not connect any form of electrical equipment to any part of the air bag circult.

# Precautions to be taken when storing an air bag unit

a Store the unit in a cupboard with the air bag upward.   
Do not expose the air bag to temperatures above 80C.   
Do not expose the air bag to flames.   
Do not attempt to dispose of the air bag consult a Citron dealer.   
e Never refit an air bag which is known to be faulty or damaged.

# De-activation of air bag system

The system must be de-activated before carrying out any work on the air bag components or surrounding area:

a Switch on the ignition and check the aperation of the air bag warning light on the instrument panel. The ight should iluminate when the ignition is switched on, then extinguish.   
Switch off the ignition.   
Remove the ignition key.   
Switch offall electrical equipment.   
Disconnect the battery negative terminal (refer to 'Disconnecting the battery' in the Reference Section of this manual.   
Insulate the battery negative terminal and the end of the battery negative lead to prevent any possibity of contact.   
Wait for at least two minutes before carying out any further work. Wait at leas ten minutes i the air bag waming light dio not operate correctly.

# Activation of air bag system

To activate the system on compietion of any work, proceed as follows:

a Ensure that there are no occupants in the vehicle, and that there are no loose jet round he iinty of the steeg wheel. Close the vefhicie doors and windows.   
Ensure that the ignition is switched off then reconnect the battery negative terminal.   
c Open the driver's door and switch on the ignition, without reaching in front of the eing whe Check hat he ir bag warning light Muminates briefly then extinguishes.   
Switch off the ignition.   
if the air bag waming light does not operate as described in paragraph c. consult a Citrodin dealer before driving the vehicle.

# General

1 The air bag sensors are integrai with the electronic control unit.

2 Any suspected faults with the air bag system should be referred to a Citron dealer - under no circumstances attempt to cary out any work other than removal and refitting of the front air bag unit(s) and/or the rotary connector, as described in the following paragraphs,

# Air bag electronic control units

3 The main ECU is located under the front section of the centre console and is accessible after removal of the console as described in Chapter 11. Each of the side air

' bags has its own ECU, fited at the base of the centre door pillar.

# Driver's air bag unit

# Removal

4 The air bag unit is an integral part of the steering wheel centre boss.   
5 De-activate the air bag system as described in Section 21.   
6 Move the steering wheel as necessary for access to the two air bag unit securing screws. The screws are located at the rear of the steering wheel boss.   
7 Remove the two air bag unit securing screws (see ilustration).   
Gentiy pul the air bag unit rom the centre of the steering wheel (see ilustration).   
Carefully unclip the wiring connector trom the air bag unit (use the fingers only, and pull the connectar upward from the air bag unit) (see llustration).   
he  io e t r length of time, refer to the storage precautions given in Section 21.

# Refitting

11 Refitting is a reversal of removal, bearing in mind the following points:

a Do not sthke the air bag unit, or expose It to impacts during refiting. b Tighten the air bag unit securing screws to the speciffed forque. On completion of refitting activate the ir bag system as described in Section 21.

# Air bag rotary connector

# Removal

12 Remove the air bag unit, as described previously in this Section.

1 Remove the steering wheel as described in Chapter 10.

14Remove the three securing screws, and withdraw the lower steering column shroud. Where applicable, manipulate the stering column adjuster lever as necessary to enable removal of the shroud.

22.17. and withdraw the rotary connector from the steering column

15 If necessary, lower the column, then unclip the upper column shroud.

16Trace the rotary connector wiring back to the connectors below the steering column and disconnect the wiring.

17 Unscrew the three securing screws, and withdraw the rotary connector from the steering column, feeding the wiring harness through the staik switch bracket (see illustrations, Note the routing of the wiing hamess.

# Refitting

1Refiting is a reversal of removal, bearing in mind the following points:

aEnsure that the rotary connector is centralised by aligning the marks on the rotary connector body and the rotating centre part prior to refitting. Instructions for centralising the unit are also provided on a lsbel on the face of the unit.   
o Ensure that the roadwheeis are in the straight-ahead position before refiting the rotary cornector and steering wheel.   
Before refitting the steering column shrouds, ensure that the rotary connector wiring harness is correctily routed as noted before removal.   
Reft the steering wheel as described in Chapter 10, and refit the air bag unit as described previously in this Section.

# Passenger's air bag unit

19 The passenger's air bag is fitted to the upper part of the facia, above the glovebox. 20 De-activate the air bag system as described in Section 21.

# Fire

• Fuel is highly lammable; fuel vapour is explosive.   
= Don't let fuel spill onto a hot engine.   
Do not smoke or allow naked lights   
(including pilot lights) anywhere near a

Another cause of fine is an electrical   
averload or short-circuit, Take care when repaining or moditying the vehicle wining.

# Special hazards

# Hydrofluoric acid

• This extremely corrosive acid is fommed when certain types of synthetic rubber, found in some O-rings, oil seals, fuel hoses etc, are exposed to temperatures above 400'C, The rubber changes into a chared or sticky substance oontaining the acid. Once formed, the acid remalns dengerous for years. If t gets onto the skin, it may be necessary to amputate the imb concemed. When dealing with a vehicle which has suffered a fire, or with components salvaged from such a vehicle, wear protective gloves and discard them after use.

# The battery

\* Asbestos dust cen cause cencer I inhaled or swalowed. Asbestos may be found in gaskets and in brake and clutch linings. When dealing with such components it is safest to assume that they contain asbestos.

# Air bags

• Air bags can cause injury if they go off accidentally. Take care whan removing the steering wheel and/or facia. Special storage instructions may apply.

# Diesel injection equipment

• Diesel injection pumps supply luel at very high pressure. Take care when working on the fuel injectors and fuel pipes,

# Remember.

# Dо

• Do use eye protection when using power tools, and when working under the vehicle. • Do wear gloves or use barrier cream to protect your hands when necessary.   
+ Do get someane to check periodically that all is wel when working elone on the vehicle,   
• Do keep loose clothing and long hair well out of the way of moving mechanical parts. • Do remove rings, wristwatch etc, before working on the vehicle - especially the   
electrical systerm.   
= Do ensure that any lifting or jacking   
equipment has a safe working load rating adequate for the job.

# DON'T

• Don't atempt to Iift a heevy component which may be beyond your capabiity - get assistance.   
• Don't rush to finish a job, or take   
unverified short cuts.   
- Don't use iI-ftting tools which may slip and cause injury.   
= Don't leave tools or parts lying around where someone can tip over them. Mop up oil and fuel spills at once.   
• Don' allow children or pets to play in or near a vehicle being worked on.

# Your Citron Xsara Manual

The aim o this manual is to help you get the best value fron your vehicle, It can do so in several ways. It can heip you decide what work must be done (even should you choose to get it done by a garage), provide information on routine maintenance and servicing, and give a logical caurse of action and diagnosis when random faults occur. However, it is hoped that you will use the manual by tacking the work yourselt. On simpler jobs it may even be quicker than booking the car into a garage and going there twice, to leave end colliect it. Perhaps most important, a lot of money can be saved by avoiding the costs a garage must charge to cover its labour and overheads,

# Choosing your engine oil

Engines need of, not only to lubricate moving parts and minimise wear, but also to maximise power output and to improve fuel economy. By introducing a simplitied and improved range of engine oils, Duckhams has taken away the confusion and made it easier for you to choose the night ol for your engine.

# HOW ENGINE OIL WORKS

# • Beating friction

Without oll the moving surtaces inside your engine will rub together, heat up and melt, quickly causing the engine to seize. Engine oil creates a fim which separates these moving parts, preventing wear and heat buld-up.

# • Cooling hot-spots

Temperatures inside the engine can exceed 1000° C. The engine ol circulates and acts as a coolant, transfering heat from the hot-spots to the sump.

# • Cleaning the engine internally

Good qualty engine oils clean the inside of your engine, collecting and dispersing combustion deposits and cantroling them unti they are trapped by the oif fiter or flushed out at oi change.

# OIL CARE - FOLLOW THE CODE

To handle and dispose of used engine ol safely, always:

. Avoid skin contact with used engine oil. Repeated or prolonged contact can be harmful.

# 1General information

This Chapter is designed to help the home mechanic maintain his/her vehicle for safety, economy, long Ie and peak performance.

# Service interval display

Certain Xsara models are equipped with a service interval display indicator in the instrument panel When the ignition is initially switched on, a spanner appears in the display window and the total number of miles remaining until the next service is due is also shown.

# Regular maintenance

1 H, from the time the vehicle is new, the routine maintenance schedule is followed closely, and frequent checks are made of fluid levels and high-wear tems, as suggested throughout this manual, the engine will be kept in reatively good running condition, and the need for additional work will be minimised. 2 It is possible that there will be times when the engine is running poorly due to the lack of regular maintenance. This is even more likaly if a used vehicle, which has not received regular and frequent maintenance checks, is purchased. In such cases, additional work may need to be caried out, outsice of the regular maintenance intervais,

# 1 General information

This Chapter is designed to help the home mechanic maintain his/her vehicle for safety, ecanomy, long life and peak performance.

# Service interval display

Certain Xsara models are equipped with a service interval display indicator in the instrument panel, When the ignition is initially switched on, a spanner appears in the display window and the total number of miiee remaining untl che next senice is due, is also shown.

# Regular maintenance

1 I, from the time the vehicle is new, the routine maintenance schedule is followed closely, and frequent checks are made of fuid levels and nigh-wear items, as suggested throughout this manual, the engine willi be kept in relatively good running condition, and the need for additional work will be minimised. 2 It is possibie that there will be times when the engine is running poory due to the lack o! regular maintenance. This is even more likely if a used vehicle, which has not received regular and frequent maintenance checks, is purchased, in such cases, additional work imay need to be carried out, outside of the regular maintenance intervals.

# Primary operations

а) Clean, inspect and test the batery (See Weekly checks).

Check the fuel fiter (Sections 4 and 17).   
Check the condition of all hoses, and check for fluid leaka (Section 5).   
Check the conditon and tension of the auxllary drivebell (Section 6).   
Check the condition of the air fiter, and renew if necessary (Section 18).

# Cooling system flushing

9 If coolant renewal has been neglected, or if the antitreeze mixture has became diluted, then in time, the cooling system may gradually lose efficlency,  as the coolant passages become nestricted due to rust, scale deposits, and other sediment. The cooling system efficiency can be restored by fiushing the system clean.

1o The radiator should be fushed independently of the engine, to avoid unnecessary contamination.

# Radiator flushing

11 To flush the radiator, disconnect the top and bottom hoses and any other relevant hoses from the radiator, with reterence to Chapter 3.

# Engine flushing

14 To flush the engine, tighten the cooling system bleed screws, then remove the thermostat (see Chapter 3). Temporarily refit the thermostat cover, without the thermostat. 1s With the top and bottom hoses disconnected from the radiator, insert a garden hose into the radiator top hose, Dinect a clean fiow of water through the engine, and continue flushing until clean water emerges from the radiator bottom hose.

# 1 General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the TU series petrai engines. Simllar information covering the XU series petrol engines, and  the  diesel engines will be found in Chapters 28 to 2D. All procedures concerning engine removal and refiting. and engine biock/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chaoters 2E and 2F as applicable,

# TU series engine description

The TU series engine is a well-proven engine wtich has been fitted to many previous Citroën and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of the in-line four-cylinder, ovemead cershaf (OHC) type, mounted Iransversely at the front of the car,  with the transmission attached to its left-hand end. The Xsara range is, fited with both 1.4 Iire (13eacc) and 1.6 itre (1587cc) versions of the engine.

1If improved access is required, fimly apply the handbrake, then jack up the front of the car and support it securely on axle stands (see Jacking and vehicle suppor). 2 Check the mounting rubber to see if it is cracked, hardened or separated from the metal at any point; renew the mounting if any such damage or deterioration is evident. 3 Check that al the mountings' fasteners are securely tightened; use a torque wrench to check if possible. 4 Using a large screwdriver or a crowbar, check for wear in the mounting by carefully levering against it to check for free play. Where this is not posslble, enlist the aid of an assistant to move the engine/transmission back-and-forth, or from side-to-side, while you watch the mounting. While some tree play is to be expected even from new components, excessive wear should be obvious. If exoessive free play is found, check first that the fasteners are secure, then renew any wom components as descrbed below.

# General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the XU series petrol engines. Similar information covering the TU series petrol engines, and the diesel engines will be found in Chapters 2A, 2C and 2D. All procedures concerning engine removal and refitting. and engine block/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

# XU series engine description

The XU series engine is a well-proven power unit which has been fited to many previous Citroin and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of the in-line four-cylinder type. mounted transversely at the front of the car with the clutch and transmission attached to its left-hand end. The Xsara range is fitted with 1.8 litre (1761cc) and 2.0 litre (1998cc) engines. Both 8and 16-valve versions of the 1.8 litre engine are avalable, whereas all 2.0 itre engines are of 16-valve configuration.

This will reduce the possibility of the engine being accidentaly cranked on the starter motor, which is likely to cause damage with the locking pins in plece.

# General information

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures for the XUD series diesel engines. Similar information covering the DW series diesel engines, and the petrol engines wil be found in Chapters 2A, 28 and 2D. Al procedures conceming engine removal and refiting, and engine block/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

# XUD series engine description

The XUD series engine is a well-proven moder unit which has appeared in many Citroän and Peugeot vehicles. The engine is of four-cylinder overhead camshaft design, mounted transversely, with the transmission mounted on the left-hand side.

# Inspection

11 Check the timing belt carefully for any signs of uneven wear, split or ol contamination. Pay particular attention to the roots of the teeth. Renew it if there is the slightest doubt about its condition. If the engine is undergoing an overhaul, and has covered more than 40 000 miles (60 000 km) with the existing belt fitted, renew the belt as a matter of course, regardless of its apparent condition. The cost of a new bet is nothing compared with the cost of repairs, should the belt break in service. If signs of oil contamination are found, trace the source of the ail leak and rectify it. Wash down the engine timing belt area and all related camponents, to remove all traces of oi. Check that the tensioner and ider pulley rotates frely. without any sign of roughness. If necessary. renew as described in Sections 9 and 10 (as applicable

# Preparation for refitting

23The mating faces of the cylinder head and cylinder block/crankcase must be perfectly clean before refitting the head. Citron recommend the use of a scouring agent for this purpose, but acceptable results can be achieved by using a hard plastic or wood scraper to remove all traces of gasket and carbon. The same method can be used to clean the piston crowns. Take particular care to avoid scoring or gouging the cylinder head/cylinder block mating surfaces during the cleaning operations, as aluminium alioy is easily damaged. Make sure that the carbon is not aliowed to enter the oil and water passages - this is particularly important for the lubrication system, as carbon could biock the

# General information and precautions

# Using this Chapter

This Part of Chapter 2 is devoted to in-car repair procedures far the DW series diesei engines, Similar information covering the XUD series diesel engines, and the petrol engines wil be found in Chapters 2A, 28 and 2C. Al procedures conceming engine removal and refitting, and engine biock/cylinder head overhaul for petrol and diesel engines can be found in'Chapters 2E and 2F as applicable.

# DW series engine description

The DW series engine is a relatively new power unit based on the well-proven XUD series engine which has appeared in many Ciron and Peugeot vehicles. The 1.9 itre (Dw8) engine is virtually identical to the 1. itre XUD unit apart from revisions to the cylinder head cover and fuel system components. The 2.0 itre (DWTD) engine i very similar to the XUD engine in terms of the cylinder block components, but the remainder of the engine has been compietely redesigned. Both engines are of four-cylinder single overhead camshaft design, mounted transversely, with the transmission mounted on the left-hand side.

# Repair operations – precaution

The 2.0 itre engine is a complex unit with numerous accessories and ancillary components. The design of the engine compartment is such that every conceivable space has been utilised, and access to virtually all of the engine components is extremely limited. In many cases, ancillary components will have to be removed, or moved to one side, and wiring. pipes and hoses will have to be disconnected or removed from various cable clips and support brackets.

# Leakdown test

9 A leakdown test measures the rate at which compressed air fed into the cylinder is lost. It is an alternative to a compression test, and in many ways it is better, since the escaping air provides easy identification of where pressure loss is occuming (piston rings, valves or head gasket).

# Preparation for refitting

18The mating faces of the cylinder head and cylinder biock/crankcase must be perfectly clean before refitting the head. Citron recommend the use of a scouring agent for this purpose, but acceptable resuits can be achieved by using a hard plastic or wood scraper to remove all traces of gasket and carbon. The same method can be used to clean the piston crowns. Take particular care to avoid scoring or gouging the cylinder head/cylinder block mating surfaces during the cleaning operatiors, as aluminium alloy is easily damaged. Make sure that the carbon is not allowed to enter the oll and water passages - this is particularly important for the lubrication system, as carbon could biock the oil supply to the engine's components. Using adhesive tape and paper, seal the water, oil and bolt holes in the cylinder block/crankcase. To prevent carbon entering the gap between the pistons and bores. smear a littie grease in the gap. After cieaning each piston, use a small brush to remove all traces of grease and carbon from the gap. then wipe away the remainder with a clean rag

25Carefully examine the cylinder head bolts for signs of damage to the threads or head. and for any sign of corrosion. If the bolts are in a satisfactory condition, measure the length of each boit from the underside of the head, to the end of the unthreaded portion at the base of the shank. The bolts may be re-used providing that the measured length does not exceed 125.5 mm. Note that, if a bolt is modified to locate the gasket (sse paragraph 27), a new bolt will be requred when finaly refitting the cylinder head. Note: Considering the stress to which the cylinder head bolts are subjected, it is highly recommended that they are all renewed. regardless of their apparent condition.

11 Examine the head of each vaive for pitting, burming, cracks, and general wear. Check the valve stem for scoring and wear ridges. Rotate the valve, and check for any obvious indication that itis bent. Look for pits or excessive wear on the tip of each valve stem. Renew any valve that shows any such signs of wear or damage.

12If the valve appears satisfactory at this stage, measure the vaive stem diameter at several points using a micrometer (see illustration). Any significant difference in the readings obtained indicates wear of the valve stem. Should any of these conditions be apparent, the valve(sj must be renewed.

1f the valves are in satisfactory condition, they should be ground (apped) into their respective seats, to ensure a smooth, gastight seal. If the seat is only lightly pitted, or if it has been re-cut, fine grinding compound only should be used to produce the required finish. Coarse valve-grinding compound shouid nor be used, unless a seat is badly bumed or deeply pitted. If this is the case, the cylinder head and valves should be inspected by an expert, to decide whether seat recutting, or even the renewal of the valve or seat insert (where possible) is required.

14 Valve grinding is carried out as fallows. Place the head upside-down on blocks, on a bench.

15 Smear a trace of (the appropriate grade of vaive-grinding compound on the seat face. and press a suction grinding tool onto the valve head (see illustration). With a semirotary action, grind the valve head to its seat, ifting the valve occasionaly to redistribute the grinding compound. A light spring placed under the valve head will greatly ease this operation.

16 If coarse grinding compaund is being used, work only until a dul, matt even surface is produced on bath the valve seat and the alve, then wipe off the used compound, and repeat the process with fine compound, When a smooth unbroken ring of light grey matt finish is produced on both the valve and seat, the grinding operation is complete. Do not grind-in the valves any further than absolutely necessary, or the seat wil be prematurely sunk into the cylinder head.

piston with the ends of the ring. The rings are brittle, and will snap if they are spread to far. They are aiso very sharp - protect your hands and fingers. 8 Look for scoring and scuffing on the piston skirt, holes in the piston crown, and burned areas at the edge of the crown. If the skirt is scored or scutfed, the engine may have been suffering from overheating, and/or abnormal combustion which caused excessively high operating temperatures. The cooing and lubrication systems should be checked thoroughly. Scorch marks on the sides of the pistons show that biow-by has occurred. A hoie in the piston crown, or burned areas at the edge of the piston crown, indicates that abnormal combustion has been occurring. If any of the above problems exist, the causes must be investigated and corrected, or the damage will occur again. # General information

The cooling system is of pressurised type. comprising a coolant pump driven by the timing belt, an aluminium crossfiow radiator, expansian tank, electric cooling fan(s), a thermostat, heater matrix, and all associated hoses and switches.

# Precautions

A Waring: Do not attempt to ea cooling system, while the engine is hot, as there is a high risk of scaiding. If the expansion tank filer cap must be removed before the engine and radiator have fuilly cooled (even though this is not recommended), the pressure in the cooling system must first be relieved. Cover the cap with a thick layer of cioth to avoid scalding, and slowly unscrew the filer cap until a hissing sound is heard. When the hissing has stopped, indicating that the pressure has reduced, siowly unscrew the filler cap until it can be removed; if more hissing sounds are heard, wait until they have stopped before unscrewing the cap. At all times, keep well away from the filer cap opening, and protect your hands.

# Fuel injection systemsgeneral information

Note: The fuel injection ECU is of the 'seitlearning' type, meaning that as it operates, it afso monitors and stores the settings which give optimum engine performance under afl operating conditions. When the battery is disconnected, these settings are iost and the ECU reverts to the base settings programmed into its memory at the factory. On restarting. this may lead to the engine running/idling roughly for a short while, until the ECU has relearned the optimum settings. This process is best accomplished by taking the vehicie on a road test (for approximately 15 minutes). covering all engine speeds and loads, concentrating mainly in the 2500 to 3500 rpm region.

# General information and precautions

# General information

The fuel system consists of a rear-mounted tuel tank, a fuel filter with integral water separator, a fuel injection pump, injectors and associated components. A turbocharger is fited to DHY (XUD9TE) and DHV (XUD9BSD) engines, together with an intercooler on the DHY unit

# Diesel electronic control systems

Primarily to comply with incrsasingly stringent emission regulations, and to alliow an engine immobiliser facility to be incorporated into the venicle _anti-theft system, all Xsara diesel engines utilise electronic contral of certain functions. 1 Checking the injection timing is not a routine operation, and should only be necessary after the injection pump has been disturbed.

# DW series engines

3 Both types of fuel injection pump (Bosch and Lucas) are fited to the DW engine by means of non-adjustable mountings. This means that the static injection timing is fixed and cannot be adjusted by rotating the pump body with respect to the engne.The only way of checking that the timing is correct is to set the engine to TDC, as described in Chapter 2, Section 3. In this position, the tming hole in the ijection pump sprocket hub should line up with a corresponding hale in the injectin pump body, allowing the fitment of a sprocket locking toal. Misalignment of the timing holes means that the timing belt has been incorectly fitted.

# 22 Electronic control system components - testing. reaaland eiting

# General information

1 All diesel engines covered in this Chapter utise slectronic control of certain functions. The number and type of sensors, actuators and associated components used on a particular engine depends on the engine type. territory of export and emission level. The tollowing information is therefore provided as a general guide to the components that may be encountered, according to engine type.

# Electronic Control Unit (ECU)

2 An ECU is used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis to contral the injection timing. preheater glow plug operation and the exhaust gas recirculation system. The ECU receives signals from sensors, which monitor engine coolant temperature, engine speed. fuel injector operation and engine load. These signals are used by the ECU to control the previously mentioned system functions.

# Crankshaft sensor

3 This is an inductive pulse generator balited to the transmission bellhousing, to scan a reference ridge on the flywheeil. As the ridge passes the sensor tip, a signal is generated, which is used by the ECU, or the EGR system, to determine engine speed. The crankshaft sensor is used on ai engines.

# Coolant temperature sensor/switch

4 The coolant temperature sensor is an NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) thermistar - that is, a semi-conductor whose electrical resistance decreases as its temperature increases. The sensor supplies a constantlyarying(analogue)voltage signal. corresponding to the temperature of the engine coolant. The sensor is used for control of the EGR system and preheating system and, on HV (XUD9BSD engine) models, is aiso used to refine the calculations made by the ECU when determining fuel metering. On some modets, the sensar consists simply of a switch whose internal contacts close once a predetermined coolant temperature has been attained.

# Throttle position switch

5 The throttle position switch is fitted to all except DHV (XUD9BSD engine) models, and s located on the top of the injection pump.

# Throttle position sensor

6 The throttle position sensor is used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis, and is located on the top of the injection pump, attached to the pump control lever. The unit consists of a potentiometer whose resistance varies according to accelerator position. From this information, the ECU can regulate the fuel injection timing according to driver input and engine load.

# Injector needle lift sensor

7 The needie lift sensor, used on DHV (XUD9BSD engine) models, is an integral part of No 3 fuel injector, and sends a signal to the ECU whenever the injector opens.

# Preheating system control unit

This unit is fitted to all models and operates the preheating system giow plugs during cold staring conditions. On DHV (XUD9BSD engine) modeis, the unit is controlled by the ECU.

When the solenoid valve is actuated (depending on coolant temperature and angine load or speed) the vacuum is diverted to the vacuum valve, thus opening the valve.

# General information and system operation

# General information

The fuel system consists of a rear-mounted fuel tank and fuel lift pump. a fuel cooler mounted under the car, a fuel titer with integral water separator, and a turbocharged, slectronically-controled High pressure Diesel injection (HD) system.

# System operation

For the purposes of describing the operation of a common rail injection system, the components can be divided into three sub-systems; the low-pressure fuel system, the high pressure fuel system and the electronic control system.

# Low-pressure fuel system

The low-pressure fuel system consists of the following components:

# High pressure fuel system

The high pressure fuel system consists of the following components:

# Electronic control system

The electronic control systern consists of the following components:

# System Components

# Fuel lift pump

The fuel Iit pump and integral fuel gauge sender unit is electrically-operated, and is mounted in the fuel tank.

# High pressure pump

The high pressure pump is mounted on the engine in the position normally occupied by the conventional distributor fuel injection pump. The pump is driven at half engine speed by the timing belt, and is lubricated by the fuel which it pumps.

# Accumulator rail

As its name suggests, the accumuliator rail acts as an accumulator, storing fuel and preventing pressure fluctuations. Fuel enters the rail from the high pressure pump, and each injector has its own connection to the rail. The fuel pressure sensor is mounted in the rail, and the rail also has a connection to the fuel pressure control valve on the pump.

# Pressure control valve

The pressure control valve is operated by the ECU, and controis the system pressure. The vaive is integral with the high pressure pump and cannot be separated.

# Fuel pressure sensor

The fuel pressure sensor is mounted in the accumulator rall, and provides very precise information on the fuel pressure to the ECU.

# Fuel injector

The injectors are mounted on the engine in a similiar manner to conventional diesel fuel injectors. The injectors are electromagnetically-operated via signais from the ECU, and fuel is injected at the pressure existing in the accumulator ral. The injectors are high-precision instruments and are manufactured to very high tolerances.

Five separate forces are essential to the operation of the injector.

# ECU and sensors

The ECU and sensors are described earier in this Section - see Electronic controi system.

# General information

All petral engines use unieaded petrol and alsa have various other features bult into the fuel system to help minimise harmful emissions. In addition, all engines are equipped with the crankcase emission control system described beiow. All engines are also equipped with a catalytic converter and an evaporative emission control system. 1.4 litre engines to emission standard L.4, aiso utise a secondary air injection system to quickly bring the catalytic converter up to naral working temperature.

The emission control systems function as follows.

# Petrol engines

# Crankcase emission control

To reduce the emission of unburned hydrocarbons from the crankcase into the atmosphere, the engine is sealed and the biow-by gases and oil vapour are drawn from inside the crankcase, through a wire mesh oi separator, into the iniet tract to be burmed by the engine during normal combustion.

# Exhaust emission control

To minimise the amount of pollutants which escape into the atmosphere, all models are fitted with a catalytic converter in the exhaust system. The system is of the closed-loop type, in which one or two lambda sensors in the exhaust system provides the engine management ECU with constant feedback. enabling the ECU to adjust the airfuel mixture ratio to provide the best possibie conditions for the converter to operate.

# Evaporative emission control

To minimise the escape into the atmosphere of unburned hydrocarbons, an evaporative emission control systerm is fitted to all models. The fuel tank filer cap is sealed and a charcoal canister is mounted undereath the right-hand wing to collect the petrol vapours generated in the tank when the car is parked. It stores them until they can be cleared from the canister (under the control of the engine management ECU) via the purge vaive into the inlet tract to be burned by the engine during normal combustion.

# Secondary air injection

Later 1.4 litre engines to emission standard L4 are also equipped with a secondary air injection system, This system is designed to reduce exhaust emissions in the period between first starting the engine, and unti the catalytic converter reaches operating (functioning) temperature. introduction of air nto the exhaust system during the initial startup period, creates an 'atterbumer' effect whicn quickly increases the temperature in the exhaust system front pipe, thus bringing the catalytic converter up to normal operating temperatures very quickly.

# Diesel engines

# Crankcase emission control

To reduce the emission of unburned hydrocarbons from the crankcase into the atmosphere. the engine is sealed and the blow-by gases anid oil vapour are drawn from inside the crankcase, through a wire mesh oil separator, into the iniet tract to be bured by the engine during normal combustion.

# Exhaust emission control

To minimise the level of exhaust pollutants released into the atmosphere, a catalytic converter is fited in the exhaust system of all models.

# Exhaust gas recirculation system

This system is designed to recirculate smal quantities of exhaust gas into the inlet tract. and therefore into the combustion process. This process reduces the level of oxides of nitrogen present in the final exhaust gas which is released into the atmosphere.

g DO NOT continue to use the car if the engine bums ail to the extent of leaving a visible trai of blue smoke.   
n) Remember that the catalytic converter operates at very high temperatures. DO NOT, therefore, park the car in dry undergrowth, over long grass or piles of dead leaves after a long run.

# General information and precautions

# General information

The engine electrical system consists mainly of the charging and starting systems. Because of their engine-related functions. these components are covered separately trom the body electrical devices such as the lights, instruments, etc (which are covered in Chapter 12). On petrol modeis refer to Part B for information on the ignition system, and on diesel models refer to Part C for information on the preheating system.

The electrical system is of the 12-volt negative earth type.

# Precautions

Further details of the various systems are given in the relevant Sections of this Chapter. While some repair procedures are given, the usual course of action is to renew the component concerned. The owner whose interest extends beyond mere component renewal should obtain a copy of the Automobile Electrical & Electronic Systems Manual, available from the publishers of this manual.

Never 'test' for altemator output by flashing' the output lead to earth.

# Ignition system - general information

# Early 1.4 and 1.6 litre engines, and all 1.8 litre (8-valve) engines

The ignition system is integrated with the fuel injection system to form a combined engine management system under the control of one ECU (See Chapter 4A for further information), The ignition side of the system is of the static (distributorless) type, consisting only of two twin-output ignition coils. The ignition coils are housed in a single unit. mounted on the left-hand end of the cylinder head; four HT leads connect the coil output terminais to the spark plugs.

# Later 1.4 and 1.6 litre engines, and all 1.8 and 2.0 litre (16-valve) engines

On these modeis, the ignition side of the system is aiso of the static (distributoriess) type and operates as described previousty. The primary difference is that the ignition coils are housed in a single unit mounted directiy above the spark plugs. The coils are integral with the spark plug caps and are pushed directly onto the spark plugs, one for each plug. This removes the need for any HT leads connecting the cois to the plugs.

# Ignition system – testing

The only ignition system checks which can be carried out by the home mechanic are those described in Chapter 1A relating to the spark plugs and. on certain modeis, the ignition coil test described in this Chapter. If necessary, the system wiring and wiring cannectors can be checked as described in Chapter 12 ensuring that the ECU wiring connectoris) have first been disconnected.
